speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
1, 2, 3 and 4. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is responsible, under section 5(1) of the Statistics Act, for the appointment of census commissoners and enumerators.

2.	(a) The purchase by Northern Transportation Company Limited of the capital stock of the aforesaid three companies cannot be properly regarded as an act of nationalization in view of the fact that the
June 6, 196S



negotiations which led to the transaction were initiated by the management and principal shareholders of the three companies. speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Mines and Technical Surveys, National Health and Welfare and Secretary of State for External Affairs as follows:

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EFFECT ON SALARIES OF CURRENT JOB RECLASSIFICATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue in his capacity as chairman of treasury board. I should like to ask the minister whether the job classification revision being done in the civil service, and particularly in the customs and excise branch, is having the effect of materially reducing the salaries of certain categories before they have had any opportunity to negotiate under the new collective bargaining legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: EFFECT ON SALARIES OF CURRENT JOB RECLASSIFICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a program of reclassification is being carried out by the Civil Service Commission. A substantial number of customs and excise officers are included in the first phase of the reclassification program, the application of which to some 50,000 civil service positions was announced a few weeks ago. In no case is the salary of an employee reduced. If the classification of a particular position is too high according to the standards established under the new classification system, the position is red-circled, which means that the employee retains his existing salary range until the established salary rates for the new classification of the position catch up. No reductions in salaries are involved.
I might point out incidentally that the reclassification is being carried on in consultation with civil service organizations which are, I understand, generally in agreement with the objectives of the program.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. subtopic: EFFECT ON SALARIES OF CURRENT JOB RECLASSIFICATION

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate I rise for the purpose of making only one point, which I wish to direct to the attention of the government by way of an objection to this kind of legislation. If I may put it without misunderstanding, I want to issue a warning that should this method be repeated in the future we will do more than record a mere objection but will do our very best by proper parliamentary means to prevent the passage of legislation in this form.
I refer, of course, to the practice incorporated in this bill of what I think can best be described as omnibus legislation; that is to say, the introduction of a single bill affecting a very large number of established statutes. This is not a new problem in this House of Commons, Mr. Speaker. We in the official opposition on a number of occasions in earlier years have recorded our very strenuous objection to this method of legislation.

I recall especially during the years 1953 to 1957. I think it is accurate to say that if hon. members will consult the Hansards of that period it will be found, generally speaking, that our objections in principle were accepted and the government of that day agreed to refrain and did in fact refrain from the practice of omnibus legislation. When our government was in office from 1957 to 1963, although I do not and cannot claim that our record was perfect in this regard, it was certainly the exception rather than the rule for any omnibus legislation to be introduced. Certainly the instances when more than one bill was affected were rare in number, and the number of bills or statutes affected by any one bill in each case were very small.
The dimensions of the problem that I am dealing with today may be recognized when it is seen that Bill No. C-178 has to do with eight new departments of government. I call them new departments because, while it is true that only six are new in name, two others, namely the Treasury Board and the Department of State are so substantially reconstituted as in effect to amount to new departments. As I say, this one bill sets up eight government departments. The same bill amends in very substantial ways five existing statutes; the Department of Public Works Act, the Department of Forestry Act, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys Act-these last two named are partially repealed-the Financial Administration Act and the Salaries Act. Then if you refer to the first part of schedule A you will find that this schedule transfer responsibility for administration of 54 statutes to new ministers or departments as compared with the present situation. Schedule B lists, in addition to the changes I have enumerated already, 30 acts which are amended or repealed in whole or in part, including the complete repeal of three existing statutes.
Mr. Speaker, surely there can be few more important pieces of legislation than those setting up new departments of government and constituting such a substantial reorganization of government administration. I submit that it is objectionable in principle and bad in practice that all those changes affecting such a wide spectrum of the operations and responsibilities of government should be incorporated in one statute. What is the man to do who is advising clients? What is the citizen taxpayer to do who wants to know, when dealing with the government, what is
June 6. 1966

Government Organization the authority and responsibility of the minister and department with whom, he is dealing? He will no longer be able to turn to the statute bearing the name of the department, in many cases. If he wants to deal with the department of energy, mines and resources he will not be able to find a statute entitled "An act respecting the department of energy, mines and resources". If he wants to deal with the Treasury Board he will not be able to refer to a statute called, perhaps, the treasury board act.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
If the citizen taxpayer wishes to deal with the Department of Forestry, or with the new department of forestry and rural development, he will not find an act entitled "The department of forestry and rural development act". I could go on through the bill giving examples of the difficulties which Canadian citizens are going to be confronted with in finding specific statutes dealing with the authorities and responsibilities of ministers or departments of government.
Sir, I might go on to speak of how the government, by this omnibus schedule consolidating and listing changes in so many acts previously administered by one minister and transferred to another, has further compounded the difficulties of the Canadian citizen. I submit that it would be most desirable if there could be in every case an appropriate statute corresponding to the name of the government department to which it refers, where the duties and responsibilities of the minister and the department will be set out. In that statute there should be the collection of acts administered by or under the responsibility of that department. This would be the proper and responsible way to legislate.
It is true that it might take a little longer to get such legislation through the House of Commons, but I doubt it. We had, in effect, six or seven separate debates at the committee stage of this bill. I doubt very much if in the over-all picture it would take appreciably longer to get the legislation through the house, were the legislation properly organized and separated as I am suggesting. And if it did take longer, Mr. Speaker, I submit that it is our responsibility as legislators and members of parliament-and it should be the responsibility of the government-to introduce legislation in that form. If doing that makes

it a little less convenient to get the legislation through the house, the government is not entitled to raise that as an excuse for imposing a very much greater inconvenience on the Canadian people.
We considered very carefully whether at this stage we should move an amendment to refer the bill back to the committee of the whole with instructions to divide it into the appropriate seven or eight parts. However, on reflection we came to the conclusion that the more appropriate course to be followed at this stage would be to register in the most emphatic terms our objection in principle to this method of legislation, and to refrain from moving an amendment at this stage.
Having served this notice, let me make it clear that should this course presently being followed be followed in future, there will be the most strenuous and, if necessary, protracted efforts to divide legislation into its component parts in order that the proper interest of both parliament and the Canadian people may be served.
On this occasion, however, I content myself, on behalf of this party and the official opposition with saying that having registered our objection, we intend to allow the bill to carry on division.

subsubtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN GOVERNMENT SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since ten o'clock last Tuesday I have been suffering the horrible frustrations of an undelivered and uncompleted speech. When the debate was adjourned I had just expressed approval, an approval in which all my colleagues on this side and my friends on the other side may well not concur, of the extension of civil service procedures and the merit system to prevailing rates employees.
Very briefly, I should like to discuss the application of the merit system as it applies in the new bill. A feature of the new bill which bothers me is the endeavour to import into the definition of merit certain selection standards based upon such factors as residence, language, age "or any other matters that, in the opinion of the commission, are necessary or desirable having regard to the nature of the duties to be performed." That clause in my opinion gives the commission the right to drive a horse and cart through the merit system. Since 1918 the merit system
June 6, 1S66

has been sacrosanct. Now the commission is given full authority to say that merit is not merit; it may be colour of eyes, curl of hair, warmth of smile or whatever the commission in its whim decides.
But let no one be under any illusion as to the desired purpose. This provision is intended to regularize what the commission has already done in importing language into merit, and all the other words are a cover. Under the old Civil Service Act such factors as residence and language were matters of job requisites, conditions precedent, if you like, to appointment. These features are retained in the new act but the new act is very different in adding something to them. Residence, language, age and other factors are made selection standards in the assessment of merit. In my view this constitutes a conflict of words. What it means is that merit is no longer merit. It is no longer to be determined by objective tests and objective standards. Merit is always to be subjective. I want to warn the government and the commission that they are embarking upon a dangerous course which may well destroy the whole merit system.
The present government policy on bilingualism in the public service is causing the most extensive demoralization I have ever seen. Anger is coupled with grave anxiety and deep consternation, and in my opinion recruitment of the best minds will fall off. I do not intend to repeat this afternoon what I said in the house on March 8. My position is very clear and unequivocal. Where performance of the work or effective service to the public requires a bilingual officer, it should be specified as a job requisite, a condition precedent, and none but bilingual persons should be appointed. But to give a preference for bilingualism in the assessment of merit for a unilingual job is a pure travesty of the merit system. The mere fact that the government has had to exempt the scientific, technical and professional fields from their policies on bilingualism is the clearest evidence of its immaturity, of its lack of present practicality, of its dangers to the whole public service.
Because I have tried to be frank and open in my approach to this problem I have been branded as anti-French. Having spent a considerable part of my life in endeavouring to bridge the gaps between races in this country, I resent that suggestion and resent it deeply. No French speaking person who has ever known me has ever believed me to be unsympathetic. Expression of realistic, honest and knowledgeable opinions in this field
Employment in the Public Service
should not lead to abuse of those persons, and I hope I am one, who will prove to understand the basis of Canadian unity best. Basic and realistic national understanding is something that I believe I can help to achieve if the political neophytes will wait until they understand the basis of Canadian unity better.
I think members of the house generally will welcome the retention of the veterans preference. It has served an important national purpose. On the other hand, the utility of the preference in its existing form is diminishing year by year and my hope would be that the special joint committee might have discussions with the Royal Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations about methods of making the theory behind the veterans preference more effective in the years ahead.
One of the fields in which the government has shown no disposition to experimentation is in the definition of political partisanship or in the definition of political rights of public servants. Representing, as I believe I do, more public servants than any other member of the house, I express my conviction that the present provisions are obsolete and unrealistic. The problem is to establish a balance between the essential impartiality, the imperative non-partisanship of the public service as a whole, and the ordinary political rights of citizenship in a democratic country.
The old act and the new act do not succeed at all in this regard. Personally I like what has been done by the legislature of Ontario and I hope the Ontario legislation, and indeed that of all other democratic jurisdictions, will be very carefully studied by the special joint committee.
This bill and all the companion bills have one general fault. The powers to enact regulations are much too broad and sweeping and the authority to delegate is much too general. The old act specified clearly and definitely the regulatory powers and in what fields those powers existed. The new act authorizes in blanket terms such regulations as may be necessary to carry out and give effect to the provisions of the act. Perhaps I was educated in the law at a time when Lord Hewart's "The New Despotism" was the popular text, but such a blanket delegation of regulatory power is an anathema to me. When this is coupled with the almost unlimited right to delegate to deputy heads it makes a total joke, if I may describe it in that way, of the old maxim upon which we were trained, namely, delegatus non potest delegare.
June 6, 1966

Employment in the Public Service
Under this bill those venerable words "civil servant" will pass from our vocabulary. On the whole I regret the passing of this designation. This nation has been brilliantly served by those who felt privileged so to describe themselves. But in the past decade the government service has undergone a vast transformation; the work has become more specialized, more complex, more technical. Each succeeding decade will accelerate that trend. In my view it is of prime importance that the new bill should give scope for growth and so that precedent may be built upon precedent.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
So, with some grave reservations which I have endeavoured to express, I support the bill and with others in this party look forward to fruitful and exhaustive discussions in the special joint committee designed to improve the bill in principle and in detail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the general outlines of the three bills with which we are dealing were first indicated to us I confess that I had some misgivings, and that some of the questions which bother the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) were of concern to me as well. However, such study as I have been able to give to the government's plans for reorganizing our public service lead me to believe that we are moving in the right direction. I look forward, along with my colleague the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), to being a member of the special joint committee which will deal with these three bills. With the two of us there I can guarantee that all the appropriate questions will be asked and I trust that some of the suggestions that we will have to make will be considered and perhaps adopted.
Nevertheless, even though there are questions to be asked and reservations to be made, I think that the general plan of dividing the problem into its three constituent parts is a good one. As I understand it, the job of deciding what kinds of people are needed and what jobs are required in the particular departments will, in the final analysis, come under the direction of the Treasury Board.
I understand that departmental heads in their capacity as managers of their functions will play a much more significant role in these decisions than has been the case in the past but that the total picture is one in which the decision as to the kind of establishment

we will have will be made under the direction of the Treasury Board. I believe this makes it possible for the set-up in our various departments to be more tailor-made to the needs of the departments, and on the whole I think this is good. In the main, of course, this function will be dealt with legislatively by the amendments that we will be making to the Financial Administration Act. They come before us under Bill C-182, the second reading of which follows this one.
Then there is the second main problem, that of staffing the various establishments. As I understand it, that is to be the main function of the public service commission which we will be appointing by the passing of Bill C-181. In so doing we are replacing the Civil Service Commission by a public service commission, and it is clear that the functions will change considerably.
At first glance it might seem that the work of the former Civil Service Commission is being greatly reduced, but I suspect that with the growing complexity of our job in the public service the job of staffing and the job of meeting our requirements will continue to grow and that the public service commission will find that it still has plenty of work to do. I also dare to believe that the more restrictive role of the public service commission will enable it to give even greater attention to the function that it must fulfil as the guardian of the merit system. Since, as I say, it will be responsible for staffing and for promotions, this will be the body that will be finally responsible for seeing to it that the merit system is intact and that both appointments and promotions are completely free of patronage, partisanship and partiality.
I was glad that the Minister of National Revenue, when he introduced this bill the other night, gave us a few minutes of history and told us something of the half century of service given to this country by the Civil Service Commission. I share his view that when that half century has been rounded out in a year or two appropriate tribute should be paid, but I think it is also proper that in the course of this debate we note with gratitude and appreciation what the Civil Service Commission itself, with the various people who have comprised it over the decades, has done both for the public service of Canada and for the building of the life of this country
As I said, Mr. Speaker, it is not just a change of name; it is a very real change we are making as we move from the era of the

We in this party have always believed that civil servants should have the same rights as other citizens of Canada. I do not believe in having second class citizens, whether on the basis of race, religion or type of employment. I am not critical of the government's intentions, which I think are excellent. We are entering a new field of legislation in this country. For the first time we are introducing legislation which spells out the right of employees to band together and bargain collectively. Of course, employees have been

banding together for many years but up till now civil service employees have had to come to the government cap in hand saying: "Please raise our pay", or "could you increase the vacation period", or "could you look into the way employees are hired and fired". The government could either agree with these requests, disagree with them or ignore them completely as it frequently did for reasons having nothing to do with the employees.
To the extent that the government now recognizes the right of federal civil servants to belong to organizations and to bargain collectively, I completely support what it is attempting to do. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the government in its desire to spell out all possibilities has brought in legislation so lengthy and so complicated that it will lead to trouble for years to come. I have had some experience with labour unions and collective bargaining, although not as much as some other hon. members. I know that the minister wishes to do a good job. We wish, however, that he had consulted the permanent officials of the federal Department of Labour and had drawn on their experience in collective bargaining. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that on the basis of available experience it has been shown that the more detailed legislation covering collective bargaining is, the more trouble you run into.
Why must we have this lengthy, detailed, extremely complicated legislation comprising three separate bills with hundreds of clauses and subclauses? Why are civil servants not treated like all other employees who come under the jurisdiction of the federal government? Why should they not be subject to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, with the same rights as employees of the railways, banks, airlines, telegraph companies or other industries which come under the jurisdiction of the federal government?
I am not trying to be critical but with the tremendous detail that the government has gone into in drafting these bills in an attempt to find answers to difficulties in advance of their arising, I submit that other difficulties have been created. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-182, to amend the Financial Administration Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we have already dealt with Bill C-170, which makes provision for a system of collective bargaining in the public service, and with Bill C-181, which makes provision for the maintenance and extension of the merit principle of appointment and promotion under an independent public service commission which would function as a central staffing agency for the public service. We come now to a measure that complements and supports the other two. I refer to Bill C-182, which proposes a number of amendments to the Financial Administration Act, amendments designed in the main to establish the Treasury Board as the central source of managerial authority in the public service and to provide it with the capacity to serve as the principal agent of the employer in the processes of collective bargaining.
Under the provisions of this bill the Treasury Board would be empowered to act for the governor in council on all matters relating to personnel management, financial management, general administrative policy and the control of organization and establishments. It would be expected in fact to concern itself generally with the quality of management in the public service.
Hon. members will recall that the lack of a central focus of managerial authority was one of the major problems identified by the royal commission on government organization and the subject of some of its most important recommendations. The provisions of Bill C-182 are wholly consistent with those recommendations.
The bill is consistent also with the Glassco recommendations that called for greater decentralization of authority to departmental management. Like the proposed public service employment act, it would make possible an extensive delegation of authority to deputy heads and other chief executive officers.
Financial Administration Act
In the view of the government the public service is becoming too complex to function efficiently without some means of giving senior departmental officers more authority to manage their affairs, within policy limits set out by the government. It should be emphasized, however, that under the proposed legislation the use of delegated authority would be subject to such conditions as the central agencies considered appropriate, and that the rights and interests of employees would be protected by the traditional appeal procedure or by the new system for the processing and adjudication of grievances.
Most of the amendments set forth in Bill C-182 are concerned with the important field of personnel management in which there has been in the past a very considerable dispersion of central authority. Under the proposed amendments, the Treasury Board would be authorized to establish policy governing almost all aspects of personnel management, including measures required to ensure effective manpower utilization, and to determine and regulate almost all conditions of employment, including classification and pay, hours of work and leave, and the standards governing physical working conditions.
The government believes that the concentration of this authority in the Treasury Board, which is essential to the proposed system of collective bargaining, will lead to a more comprehensive and co-ordinated approach to the planning and development of personnel policy than any that has been possible in the past.
It will be noted that some of the amendments are designed to transfer to the Treasury Board functions now located in whole or in part in the Civil Service Commission. For example, the commission now has responsibility for the maintenance and administration of the system of classification and pay applying to civil servants. Because rates of pay will be subject to collective bargaining and arbitration, and because classification is in a sense the process whereby employees are grouped for purposes of salary administration, it is essential that this responsibility be transferred.
It will be noted that other amendments are designed to give the board authority to establish conditions of employment that are now fixed by statute in so far as civil servants are concerned. I am referring here to hours of work, leave and holidays, all of which will be matters falling within the scope of collective bargaining and arbitration.
6012	COMMONS
Financial Administration Act
In other circumstances the concentration in the Treasury Board of authority to determine and regulate conditions of employment might have been regarded with apprehension by employees. At a time when bargaining rights are being granted and steps taken to establish formal grievance procedures, I doubt that this will be the case. Indeed, I think there is a recognition on the part of most, if not all, organizations representing public servants that, if there is to be genuine collective bargaining, some one agency must be able to speak with authority for the employer, the government of Canada.
In addressing myself to this bill and its companion measures I have attempted to describe the principles underlying the program of legislation developed by the government to provide for the introduction of collective bargaining, the retention of the merit system of appointment and promotion and a redistribution of managerial authority along lines recommended by the royal commission on government organization. Much more could be said but in view of the plans to subject all three measures to careful scrutiny by a joint committee I doubt that the time required could be justified. In conclusion, let me repeat what I have already said in the earlier debates. This is legislation of great importance, perhaps the most important legislation of its kind that has been laid before this house since the Civil Service Act of 1918 established the foundations for a great and impartial public service. I know that hon. members will wish to give to it the attention and careful study that it deserves when it is referred to the appropriate committee.
Hon. n. A. Bell (Carleion): Mr. Speaker, in the debate on the two accompanying bills I dealt indirectly with the principle of this bill and with its prov sions as they affect the public service. Personally I do not see how expenditures can realistically be divorced from taxation policies, and that is what happens when you separate Treasury Board completely from the Department of Finance.
I just do not appreciate how you can divorce supply and ways and means. Rumour hath it that the Carter commission will propose abandonment of the Department of National Revenue as a ministerial portfolio and the handing over of the collection process to some type of board of commissioners of internal revenue. If this be true, I am inclined to say "a plague on both royal commissions." The other tidying-up operation in this bill repeals and then re-enacts the provisions for governor general's warrants. I confess that I
June 6, 1966
was brought up in the old school which believed that governor general's warrants were evil per se and basically inconsistent with responsible government. I do not believe that provisions for them should be re-enacted in their present form. By introducing this clause in the bill I think the government has raised the whole issue of the future use of governor general's warrants. In this respect I emphasize that I speak only for my myself, but I believe it is an affront to parliament and responsible government for a prime minister to dissolve the house without having secured from parliament financial provision for at least the election period. Mr. Speaker, I want to voice certain reservations about some of the principles underlying the bill before the house, but they do not follow the reservations voiced by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). As I understand what the minister has said and what the bill says-I ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong-in the context of the total legislation with which we are concerned Bill No. C-170 makes Treasury Board the bargaining agent, as it were, on behalf of the government. As I understand the changes proposed in Bill No. C-182, they are by and large intended to give Treasury Board the powers it needs in order to conclude a collective agreement with the bargaining agents which are set up under Bill No. C-170. I therefore cannot but agree on behalf of our party with the general proposition that if Treasury Board is going to do the bargaining it must have the authority to make an agreement when the bargaining is over. You cannot possibly have Treasury Board as the bargaining agent and then leave 23033-38U
Financial Administration Act with the public service commission the authority to make decisions.
I think this is the basic purpose of the bill and with that purpose, if one has any understanding of the process of collective bargaining, one is forced to agree. I have done a great deal of collective bargaining in 15 or 16 years of labour law work, and there is nothing more frustrating in a collective bargaining process than to sit opposite the bargainer on behalf of the employer who has no authority to tell you what the employer is really intending to do. The change in this respect is, in my submission, desirable despite the views which the hon. member for Carleton expressed.
But, Mr. Speaker, I see in all three bills with which we have been concerned a continuing tendency on the part of those who have advised the government not to let go of the traditional powers of government. Let me say that you cannot have collective bargaining in private industry unless management is prepared at some point to abridge the ordinary common law authority of management; and you cannot have collective bargaining with a government unless the government is prepared to abridge the ordinary constitutional powers which it normally has. You cannot have collective bargaining if the government insists that it will remain the final authority despite the collective bargaining process, and you cannot have genuine collective bargaining if you retain legally in the hands of the government agency the final word about what is to happen. When you have that you do not have collective bargaining.
The first thing, therefore, that worries me immensely about Bill No. C-182 is precisely what the minister referred to, namely, that one of the clauses of the bill retains in the hands of Treasury Board without qualification and, on the contrary, specifically, the authority, notwithstanding any other provision of any other enactment, to determine everything that normally goes into collective bargaining. It retains the authority to determine the requirements for and terms of training, the classification of positions and employees, the authority to determine and regulate pay, to determine and regulate hours of work and leave of employees, the power to establish physical working conditions and things related thereto, the power to determine and regulate payments in connection with travelling expenses and allowances and

6014	COMMONS
Financial Administration Act if that were not enough, the power to determine all other terms and conditions of employment which are not mentioned specifically.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It may have been the intention of the government that Treasury Board have these powers in order to be able to implement the terms of a collective agreement reached with the bargaining agent. The minister nods his head. As a lawyer let me say to him, if I may: If that is what he intended, that is what he ought to have said. The bill says nothing of the sort. The bill does not say that this authority which is retained by the Treasury Board, and which may in certain circumstances be delegated to someone else, is subject to the collective bargaining process and to any collective bargaining agreement reached. It merely gives that authority, unqualified and without reservation, to the Treasury Board.
The point that one must always remember in collective bargaining is that if a representative of the employees sits at a bargaining table he will only be able to bargain if he feels that he is the equal of the people who sit opposite him. So long as the people who sit opposite him in the collective bargaining process have in their hands the ultimate weapon to deprive him of genuine collective bargaining, so long as the people who sit opposite him and who represent the employer are able to say directly or by implication, we have the authority to impose this on you if you do not like it in the last resort, so long as that is the situation and so long as the law reads that way, genuine collective bargaining does not take place
The wrong principle embodied in this bill is that the authority which is to be given to the Treasury Board in order to enable it to implement a collective agreement is given in such a way that it can exercise that authority as far as the law is concerned without regard for the collective bargaining process. It is my intention, as it is that of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, to do everything we can to make sure that this is remedied in the legislation.
A thought occurred to me, Mr. Speaker, as I was speaking. Suppose the parties at the collective bargaining table reach an impasse, suppose the bargaining agent has chosen, under Bill C-170, the role of conciliation rather than of compulsory arbitration and suppose the situation in Canada is such that the

government feels it cannot tolerate the possibility of a strike. Then Treasury Board has the power under Bill C-182-and we understand the minister will be president of the Treasury Board at that time-to impose conditions which should otherwise be bargained for collectively.
I am confident, as we all have said, that the minister's intention and the intention of his government is to introduce collective bargaining. If we are mistaken in that, if they have any reservations on that point and we are really beating the air, it would be a heartbreaking fact. However, I am assuming they really intend to introduce genuine collective bargaining. If that is the case, I plead with them to get rid of the chains which now bind their minds concerning the ultimate power being in the hands of the employer because in this case the employer happens to be the government. We simply will not have collective bargaining for the benefit of the people concerned so long as there is this hidebound approach to the relationship with the employees.
The same is true of the appeal procedure. The minister said in the earlier debate that the public service commission will be an independent body and will not be government controlled. Of course no one is suggesting that the Civil Service Commission has been a government agency which has carried out government orders or anything of the sort. But the fact is that the public service commission has certain duties under this legislation, as the Civil Service Commission had under the other legislation.
Its duties are, in the first place, to make appointments, to give promotions and to make certain decisions with regard to the conditions of work in certain spheres. The body which makes the decision about employment, promotion, demotion and all the rest of it is not the body that should have the final say in the appeal procedure. In the same way the Treasury Board under this bill is the body which makes certain regulations with regard to discipline and other things. It should not be the final appeal board. The fact that we request the minister to consider making appeals subject to the agreement procedure of the collective bargaining process is not to be taken as throwing barbs at the public service commission or questioning the impartiality or the best intentions of that body. We ask for independent arbitration because the public service commission is inevitably and necessarily directly concerned
June 6, 1966

with the decisions against which the employees are protesting. The body which in the first place makes the decision cannot be the body which in the last resort should decide the appeal. It is as simple as that.
May I also say to the minister and to his advisers that the essence of trade unionism is frequently misunderstood. It is often taken for granted that the major object of a union is merely to get an increase in wages or a reduction in hours or some additional physical or monetary benefits for the people concerned. That is certainly an important part of the organization of labour. However, Mr. Speaker, I say to you and to the minister that even more important than all of the monetary benefits which a union seeks to achieve is the fact that it is the spokesman of the employees who otherwise would not have their own spokesman. It is much more important for the member of a union or the member of a bargaining unit represented by a union that his organization be able to represent him, to fight for him when he thinks he has been aggrieved, to take his case right up to the final arbitral tribunal, than it is for the employee to get another 5, 10 or 15 cents an hour. Both in the federal service and in ordinary industry the single employee is a number, whether he punches the clock or signs the book and, left alone, the employee when he feels himself aggrieved cannot do anything that is adequate to protect himself.
The major value of the trade union in the democratic and social sense is that it is the spokesman and protector, on an equal basis with the employer, of the employee whenever he feels himself aggrieved by any act of the employer. This is why we in this party are concerned about the principles which seem to animate the three pieces of legislation that are before us. At the same time, as I said on an earlier occasion, while dotting every "i" and crossing every "t" in the proposed collective bargaining legislation we retain unreserved and unqualified power in the hands of management, in this case the governor in council, the Treasury Board or the public service commission, which, if it were applied as the wording of the legislation enables it to be applied, would rob the collective bargaining process of any meaning.
The second principle with which I wish to deal very briefly is the one about which we had so much fuss in parliament in connection with the late Mr. Spencer. I am astonished that the amendments to Financial Administration Act as contained in this bill not only
Financial Administration Act leave the old section 50 of the Civil Service Act unchanged except in one respect, namely, limiting the power to dismiss without appeal for the safety and security of Canada, but this time spell it out in the bill instead of it being understood as was the case before. In essence there is no change in section 50 by this bill but in fact it is made worse. It says in so many words that once there is a piece of paper dismissing an employee of the government allegedly for reasons of security and safety it becomes final proof that the employee is unsafe from the point of view of the security of Canada. What makes it even worse is that the bill spells out in the clearest possible terms the fact that once the employee is thus dismissed he is through. He cannot question the reason for the dismissal because the piece of paper, it seems to me, is final proof of the fact he is a security risk for Canada.

When we had the debate on the Victor Spencer matter my impression was that there were members on the government side, indeed members of the cabinet, who agreed that there ought to be an amendment to section 50 of the Civil Service Act, who agreed that there ought to be some appeal from such dismissal. Unless my memory serves me wrongly, and I have not gone back to Hansard to check on the matter, these hon. members opposite emphasized the fact that the only reason they had to support the government on the Spencer issue was that there was the law, there was section 50. They said that it had to be applied in a case like Mr. Spencer's.
Surely this was the opportunity for the government to rectify that situation. When we are re-evaluating all the legislation relating to civil servants in Canada, this bill was the means whereby the government could have provided for a hearing. If that is the reason, Mr. Speaker, I cannot think of anything more invalid than to say that a necessary amendment has to wait upon the report of a board of inquiry that has not been set up yet. I see no reason whatever for waiting. The government could have proposed an amendment that would give a person dismissed as a security risk the right, if he desired it, to a
June 6, 1966

Financial Administration Act full and impartial inquiry by a commissioner or commissioners appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act or by any other body the government thought more capable of looking into the matter.
I must admit to profound disappointment, after what parliament went through in the Spencer case and even after the Prime Minister had granted a commission of inquiry in that case, allegedly I understand because the late Mr. Spencer asked for it, because I cannot for the life of me understand what it was that prevented the government from including an amendment that would make an impartial inquiry a matter of right for any employee of the government dismissed under section 50 of the Civil Service Act. It is the intention of those who represent this party on the joint committee to suggest amendments to the legislation which will make it clear that any powers granted the Treasury Board are subject to the collective bargaining process and cannot be exercised in order to interfere with that process. We intend to propose also an amendment to this legislation which will give any person dismissed, for whatever reason but including the reason of security, an opportunity for a full and impartial hearing.

[Mr. Lewis.)

the decision made by his employer-in the Spencer case the government. Whether an appeal should be heard in public or in private, Mr. Speaker, is not the issue at this point. In other places the minister will be the president of the Treasury Board.
Financial Administration Act

Clause 3 of the amending bill, which amends existing section 7 of the Financial Administration

Financial Administration Act Act, was put into the bill so that the powers accorded throughout numerous other pieces of legislation could be drawn in under this piece of legislation; it was not put in so as to override any decision with regard to collective agreements.
The second point which he raised is a difficult one, and that is the matter of dismissal of people in the interests of the safety and security of the nation, the so-called security cases. This is a matter to which I should like to assure him we gave a great deal of thought as to what we should do. Perhaps the commission's report will make a recommendation as to how security cases should be dealt with, how far security matters should be divulged, what types of hearings should be held in security cases, and the particular matters which are involved in any appeal which might be allowed with respect to cases coming under section 50.
The hon. member has the right, of course, to disagree with the decision of the government and I would be very surprised if in most instances he did not do so. However, the decision of the government was that the clause should be put in with the strict limitation that it will apply only to security cases, which was not the case before. We really had doubt whether we should even put in that provision because if someone is discharged under the section people will automatically know that a security case is involved. So to that extent perhaps you are branding someone by dismissing them under the section.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
However, the government decided to await the decision of the royal commission which had been set up to look into security procedures. Certainly everyone will have the opportunity of making his views known fully with regard to this matter when it goes before the committee. The government will, of course, consider the views put forward by various hon. members when the particular bill is considered by the special committee of the house and the Senate.
I now wish to deal briefly with matters raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with respect to the drafting of changes in the Financial Administration Act. I was concerned about the drafting and about having two ministers under one particular bill, which would be the

case in the Financial Administration Act. Although the Treasury Board has been mentioned there is quite a change in the position of the Treasury Board, and the president of the Treasury Board comes under the bill. I was assured that the drafting of this bill had been undertaken with the greatest care possible under the circumstances by officials in the Department of Justice.
The hon. member asked for the philosophy behind the division of duties between the president of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance. If the hon. member refers to the report of the Glassco commission I think he will see set out clearly what that commission recommended with respect to the president of the Treasury Board. It recommended that the post of president of the Treasury Board be created to deal basically with government expenditures. In other words, the president of the Treasury Board would be responsible for such things as the approval of departmental estimates and for applying directives laid down by the governor in council or cabinet and would look into such matters as organization within departments, improving and upgrading employees in the public service with respect to operating the public service more efficiently, taking an over-all look-and this would be done by the Treasury Board reporting through its president-at the organization of government. This means that the field of supply involving the moneys necessary to make government expenditures falls into the lap of the president of the Treasury Board.
It might seem at first, and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) mentioned this, that Treasury Board would run off in one direction and the Minister of Finance in another. I assure hon. members, nevertheless, that Treasury Board is not the president of the Treasury Board. Treasury Board consists of a number of ministers including the Minister of Finance. The president of the Treasury Board has the burden of looking after the detail of expenditures, dealing with departmental and governmental organization, and he must look after the upgrading of the organization, trying to improve efficiency within the government organization. That job, in the opinion of the Glassco commission, was too detailed and cumbersome to be put on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance is basically responsible for economic policy, for monetary policy generally in the country, and, indeed, for many other matters.
June 6, 1966



Indeed, there must be close liaison between the president of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance. I can assure hon. members that the concept of having a president of the Treasury Board as well as a minister of finance could not work if there were not close liaison between the two. Government could not work if there were not close liaison between, say, the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. There has to be liaison and consideration of each other's problems as between all ministers of government or the government will not work but disintegrate, as has sometimes happened in the past.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I trust that the words of admonition used by the hon. member for Kamloops this afternoon on the subject of omnibus bills do not apply to the measure contemplated in the resolution before us, because if ever a bill was an omnibus bill the bill to be introduced following this resolution will be one. This has to be the case because a great many acts will have to be changed in order to make possible integration with the Canada Pension Plan. In most cases the amendments to the various acts will be the same but they must be brought about by an omnibus bill.
Perhaps before we complete our discussion on the resolution we might hear the views of hon. members on this subject. This is certainly not an omnibus bill of the type to which objection was taken earlier today, but there

needs to be amendment of between 15 and 20 acts affecting people in various parts of the public service.
The main purpose of this resolution is to make possible the introduction of legislation to provide for co-ordination between the Canada Pension Plan and a number of acts dealing with the superannuation of members of the public service. It is highly desirable that the amendments to the various acts mentioned in the resolution should come into effect at the same time; consequently, the government felt it would be desirable to proceed by means of a statute law amendment bill which would combine all of the proposed legislative amendments in a single bill.
When the bill to establish the Canada Pension Plan was before the house a detailed explanation of the government's proposals, designed to co-ordinate the Public Service Superannuation Act with the Canada Pension Plan was given both to the house itself and to the joint parliamentary committee which reviewed that bill. The legislation which this resolution contemplates contains the provisions Which were foreshadowed and explained at that time.
It will be recalled that the joint parliamentary committee on the Canada Pension Plan suggested that the door should be left open, if possible, for integration of the Canada Pension Plan with the existing pension provisions covering the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. The committee recommended that the "provision exempting the armed services and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police from coverage under the Canada Pension Plan should, if integration is technically feasible, be deleted". While a satisfactory method of integration could not be developed before the Canada Pension Plan was passed, section 6(2)(g) of the bill to establish that plan was amended in committee to conform to the joint committee's view. The clause as amended now provides that excepted employment is "employment as a member of the Canadian forces or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police except as provided by any other act of the parliament of Canada". During the intervening months a method of integration has been developed which meets the criteria established by the joint parliamentary committee in the case of persons to whom the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act apply. This bill will, therefore, implement the recommendations of the joint committee to the greatest feasible extent.
June 6. 1966

In the explanation which has already been given to the house and to the joint parliamentary committee on the general method of co-ordination or correlation which is proposed with respect to the public service, R.C.M.P. and armed forces legislation, two basic criteria have been set forth. The first principle is that the total contributions paid by the employee and by the government on the salary on which contributions are now being paid under the relevant superannuation acts should not be increased; instead a portion of the contributions should be diverted away from the superannuation fund in each case to the Canada Pension Plan or to the Quebec Pension Plan in the case of those persons who are employed in the province of Quebec.
As a consequence of this diversion it was recognized that the benefits earned under the relevant superannuation act would have to be reduced. This led to the second principle, namely, that the reduction in benefits should not bring the total level of benefits below the level that would have prevailed under the superannuation act had it not been for the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan. Thus the total contributions would not increase and the total benefits would not decrease, and might even be marginally increased in some instances, in the case of present employees who take their retirement in future either on grounds of age or disability. In addition, their pension credits already earned for service prior to the commencement of the Canada Pension Plan would not be affected.
As hon. members realize, it was not possible to introduce this legislation prior to January 1, 1966, so that in order to prevent a decrease in the take-home pay of those civil servants who were already contributing 5 or 6| per cent of their salary to the superannuation account it was necessary to provide accountable advances to cover the period until this legislation was introduced and passed. These accountable advances have been made to date under the authority given by parliament by vote LlOOd of the Appropriation Act No. 2, 1966 and vote LlOOe of the Appropriation Act No. 4, 1966. The effect of the provision contained in this present bill would be to reduce the amounts which such persons are required to contribute to the superannuation account with effect from January 1, 1966 so that the advances made to persons who are contributing on the date of royal assent will be recovered in this way.
Pensions
Similar provisions will apply to those public officials who are contributing under the Diplomatic Service (Special) Superannuation Act. No such provision was necessary in the case of the members of the Canadian forces or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police since they have not been required to contribute under the Canada Pension Plan up to the present time. However, Canadian National Railways has arranged for similar advances in the case of those employees to whom the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways Employees' Provident Fund Act applies.
Quite apart from the arrangements for integration with the Canada Pension Plan, the bill contains a number of other amendments which have been deferred until the present time, principally because the pressure of legislative business did not give parliament an earlier opportunity of dealing with them. Some of these relate to proposals of the public accounts committee; others arise from recommendations contained in the quinquennial actuarial reports on the various superannuation and death benefit accounts; others reflect the growing interest in the question of portability of pension rights and are designed to broaden the provisions of certain of the acts in this regard.
Finally, a number of the amendments are proposed for the purpose of taking care of anomalies and administrative problems which have come to light during the years since these acts were last before parliament for a detailed review. I should mention that the references to the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act and the Canadian Corporation for the 1967 World Exhibition Act are included for this last reason and not because of any direct connection with the Canada Pension Plan.
At this stage I would like to make particular mention of two items out of the general categories which I have just outlined. One of these is mentioned in the resolution and has for its purpose the raising of the limit under the supplementary death benefit plan for members of the public service and the Canadian forces which is presently provided under Part II of the Public Service Superannuation Act. It is proposed to raise this limit from the present ceiling of $5,000 to the approximate actual salary or pay level of the person concerned, subject to the continuation of the present provision by which the total death benefit is reduced by one-tenth of the basic benefit each year after reaching the age
June 6, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of 60, and to the retention of the minimum benefit of $500 for those to whom this has applied in the past.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The low level of the death benefit under this plan was a subject of comment by the Glassco commission. At the same time it is proposed, for administrative and other reasons, to delete from part II of the Public Service Superannuation Act the provisions affecting members of the regular forces and to add a new part III to the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act to provide for the continuation of death benefit coverage for present members of the Canadian forces and former ones who are covered by this plan.
Finally, I would like to mention that the government has been concerned for some time over the rigid limitations, contained in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act, on the amount of pension a former officer may receive under those acts if he is subsequently employed in the public service of Canada. The bill contains a provision which will make this control more flexible. This provision is similar to that contained in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act which leaves it to the governor in council to deal with this situation by regulation.

subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, immediate steps should be taken by the government to arrange for a federal-provincial highway building conference at the earliest possible moment in order that a national highway building program be instituted with special attention in such a program to be given to access roads in the northern areas and lesser developed areas of the nation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the age of federal-provincial conferences. In recent years we have had these conferences on a variety of subjects and some of them were fruitful and others were not. What the motion seeks is to have a national highway building conference established, something which, incidentally, was contemplated and planned when Hon. Jean-Paul Deschatelets was the minister of public works. In fact, while he was minister he had so organized and arranged the plans for a dominion-provincial conference on highways that the date for it was almost established.
Unfortunately, however, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the then minister of finance, at a dominion-provincial fiscal conference in Quebec city, gave way to some of the demands of that province and as a result the then minister of public works, Mr. Deschatelets, had to come to parliament and regretfully announce that the plan for a dominion-provincial highway building conference had been cancelled because, as he put it, there was not sufficient money to go around inasmuch as there had been an increase in the contribution under the tax-sharing arrangement. In any event, at that time there was a recommendation with regard to the responsibility of the federal government in the field of highway building, a recommendation with which I agree, namely, that the federal government must participate in a national highway building program in order that there might be an orderly development of highways and roads in this nation.
I think this was recognized at least tentatively in 1949 when the Trans-Canada Highway Act was passed and that highway was contemplated. It was also recognized when the Conservative government took office by the establishment of the so-called roads to resources program under which the federal and provincial governments participated jointly in financing roads which led to potential or actual natural resources or which
June 6, 1966

Highways
opened up areas particularly in the northern part of our nation.
We would hope that the ideas conceived with regard to those two forms of financial participation could be carried forward. Since 1949 there has been quite in increase in travel, in the ownership of automobiles and in the expansion of the nation in respect of population and affluence. There has been a heavy emphasis upon tourism, upon seeing Canada, and a heavy highway building program has been instituted in the various provinces. In order to develop it is necessary that we try to co-ordinate and tie together the various highway building programs in the provinces. This means that there must be more communication and preparation on a national basis. In the motion I place emphasis on the northern part of our nation because we all know that in the highly populated southern areas of Canada the population itself creates sufficient pressure on the provincial governments with relation to the building of highways at least.
We conceive that with the federal government participating financially it would be the dominant force in respect of highways in those parts which are not so well populated. We conceive also of the necessity for opening up areas which now are not populated at all or, if so, only to a very limited extent. We believe that roads which open up areas automatically bring people there for settlement and for the exploitation of the resources which exist there, and people bring prosperity.
I should like to make only passing reference to the portion of British Columbia from which I come. For some years we have had an intensive interest in the concept that what locally in the province is referred to as highway 16, which extends from there through the Rocky Mountain trench area to Jasper, should be part of another trans-Canada highway. Incidentally, this proposal has received unanimous political support at the local level for as long as I can remember. The Liberal party revises its support for this program every time there is an election, but promptly forgets about it when the election is over. I should like those hon. members who raise their eyebrows at this statement to remember that fact, because it is a fact. We are not interested at home in merely making political hay out of roadbuilding programs; we want to see something worthwhile accomplished in this regard.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
Because the provincial governments have some jurisdiction over the building of highways and because the federal government is involved both jurisdictionally and actually in the building of highways in the Northwest Territories and has an overriding responsibility for the development of an orderly highway system we think that a conference is necessary. Co-operation is needed between the various levels of government, and at such a conference it would be possible to set out those areas which require a roadbuilding program. It would also be possible to come to some agreement about the money split-who would pay how much toward what.
We believe that priorities are necessary so that we can engage in the building of highways that are urgently needed and we feel it is possible to establish priorities at a federal-provincial conference. In this way the provinces would know on the basis of long-range plans what to expect in the way of federal financial participation and could plan accordingly.
I rather anticipate that this motion will not receive different treatment from that accorded to similar motions which come before the house and that a Liberal backbencher will be on his feet at the end of private members' hour loving this particular motion to death. If that is the desire of the Liberal party I wish them Godspeed, but if there is a real and genuine desire to treat me gently hon. members will let this motion come to a vote so that parliament can at least give an expression of opinion on this extremely urgent question.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. B. Stewart (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) is one that I am sure will recommend itself to members in all parts of the house. He has referred to the need for better roads and highways throughout Canada and we all applaud that goal. The next immediate step proposed by the hon. member toward the achievement of better roads and highways from a federal point of view is the convening of a federal-provincial highway building conference. While I think we would agree with the aim he puts forward, I for one would disagree with his suggestion that such a conference is the next logical step, and I want to submit to the house through you, Mr. Speaker, certain reasons for taking that view.

June 6, 1966
Highways
Before doing that I want to agree with the hon. member that there is no question but that the government of Canada is thoroughly involved in the matter of roads and highways. The hon. member very cautiously mentioned the years 1949 and 1958, but I should think one could go back beyond that time to the Canada Highways Act and to some of the things that were done in the 1930's, perhaps primarily to relieve unemployment but certainly with a direct effect on highways.
In so far as the roads to resources program begun in 1958 is concerned, this was, if you will, a flowering of a process which goes back something like 30 years in respect of forest access roads and the like. There is no question but that the government of Canada is thoroughly involved in highway construction, but what is now before us is a question regarding means, and I suggest that the immediate desirable step to be taken is not what is proposed in this motion.
The hon. member put his motion on the order paper on January 20, 1966, and I am sure at that time he did not anticipate certain circumstances as they now exist. I want to suggest that the desirability of an immediate conference in this period of great instability and uncertainty of provincial government is at least questionable. Earlier today the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) told the house that the timing of the announced federal-provincial conference which is to concern itself with financing in the field of education was somewhat uncertain by reason of the prevailing instability and uncertainty of provincial government, so I think this is not the opportune time for the immediate launching of yet another federal-provincial conference. Perhaps that is somewhat facetious, for I am sure the hon. member would be prepared to let this proposal stand until such time as things are somewhat more stable in the field of provincial government.
We must consider the question of the usefulness of the proposed highway building conference. Let us look at some of the programs in which the government of Canada has been participating directly or indirectly. First, we have the matter of highway construction in the north. If the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) were speaking now I am sure he would refer to an announcement he made last October to the effect that the government of Canada, in order to stimulate resources development in Canada's north, was launching

upon a massive ten year roadbuilding program in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. This new program calls for an average expenditure of $10 million per year and is to be carried on for a long period. This is an area which would not need to be touched upon at least by a federal-provincial conference, and I mention it initially so as to put it aside.
The trans-Canada highway collaboration between Canada and the provinces has been a major adventure in highway construction, and we all know that the first trans-Canada highway has not as yet been completed. Only last year on August 2 the Prime Minister announced that the final date for payment to the provinces for trans-Canada highway construction was to be extended until December of 1970. That was the government's proposal. It is interesting to note that there is a good deal of work yet to be done on this first trans-Canada highway. I have some figures at hand but I will not try to put them before the house just now. There is a good deal of work to be done in the province of Quebec and Nova Scotia. Both of these provinces are pushing ahead with this work and I assume will be able to complete it within the new time limit. However, I think it would be premature actually to launch a second trans-Canada highway until we have managed to wrap up the first one.
One must also consider the roads to resources program and the fact that this also is not completed. I understand that there is considerable money available from the government of Canada in the case of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan and British Columbia under the roads to resources program. This was not a large program. The money available to each of the several provinces was $7J million, but in certain cases not all this money has been used. I understand that when a revival or continuation of this program is discussed, what comes to the fore is the need to appraise what has been done. It may very well be that in some instances the fullest value has not been obtained and consequently that some new specifications should be introduced on how this kind of money should be spent.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
Then there is the other question which presumably would make a nice point for discussion and ratification at a federal-provincial conference, namely, the distribution of money and whether each of the several provinces should get exactly the same amount
June 6, 1966

regardless of population, size and the engineering difficulties of the terrain. My understanding is that although the roads to resources program has not yet been completed, thought is being given to questions such as those to which I have just referred.
I have looked over some of the comments the hon. member for Skeena has made in the past on this interesting subject. On one occasion he was very intrigued by the work being undertaken by the Atlantic Development Board in connection with trunk highway construction in the Atlantic provinces. If I recall correctly, he applauded this program, and so do we all. This is a good undertaking. We are hoping that as these trunk highways begin to make their impact on our Atlantic economy they will contribute greatly to the general economic well-being of our area and will help solve some of the problems that exist in this regard. However, Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of work to be done. I notice, for example, that my own province of Nova Scotia has only begun to use that money. Here again we have, as it were, a great deal of unfinished business.
What I have been doing, Mr. Speaker, is to refer to some of the aspects of federal participation in road and highways construction and to suggest that several of these programs are still in operation although it is true that they are in their tapering-out stages. I would not lean on this argument as conclusive in dealing with the motion put forward by the hon. member for Skeena. There is another point that I think is very important. I refer to the work being done by the tax structure committee.
We are all familiar with the problem that prevails, namely, that of the provinces having jurisdiction and Canada having at least the legal right to tax. I think it would be unwise to launch now a federal-provincial conference on highway building, which I suggest must go ahead on the presumption that the federal government will continue in much the same way as it has in the past, that is, making grants in aid in connection with highway projects, until such time as the tax structure committee has made its report and until such time, indeed, as the appropriate constitutional authorities have accepted or rejected the proposals of that committee. We should not anticipate that report.
I understand that consultation regarding various aspects of highway transportation does go on between provincial and federal
Highways
officials. The provincial authorities raise various questions on highway transportation. I would think it is fair to assume that the whole range of questions adduced by the motion of the hon. member for Skeena is being and will be explored in these conversations. I would hope that as these conversations, albeit at the official level, go on the thinking of Canadians with regard to Canada's highway needs would develop and become modernized. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I am suggesting that there probably is going on, if you will subterraneously, talk and thinking which may very well at the appropriate time eventuate in the kind of conference the hon. member is now proposing.
Therefore my concluding remark is that I think the aim of the motion is commendable but that I do not think a federal-provincial highway building conference at the earliest possible moment, as contemplated by the motion, is the best next step toward the accomplishment of the aim the hon. member has in mind.
