subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is wonderful this afternoon to find the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) introducing a motion for the convening of a conference on highways to consider the development and expansion of the north because those members who come from British Columbia value very highly the highways systems of this country and of their own province in particular. We live in an extremely mountainous province, one in which access to its great resources is extremely difficult and very costly to achieve with the result that we have to do so slowly. Fortunately we have been aided in our development by two outside sources. One source has been the federal government which has not only built the trans-Canada highway but has also assisted in the building of additional 
routes through the federal parks within that province and also under the roads to resources program.
In addition to the assistance from the federal government considerable assistance has also been given to the development and expansion of northern British Columbia in the form of U.S. funds that were put into the building of the Alaska highway from Dawson Creek to Alaska, which was a military route during world war II.
In addressing myself to the motion of the hon. member I want to dwell for a moment on the importance of this highway and on what should be considered by any federal-provincial conference on roads in respect of that highway. If you go north out of Vancouver up to the centre of the province, a distance of approximately 500 miles, you come to the city of Prince George which is pretty well in the centre of the province of British Columbia. From Prince George you take the Hart highway, named after a former premier of that province, for a distance of approximately 270 miles north and slightly east to the town of Dawson Creek, not to be confused in the minds of easterners with Dawson City which does not lie in the province of British Columbia. Dawson Creek lies in the Peace river district, a great farming district opened up in northern Alberta and British Columbia, access to which is not only by the Hart highway from Prince George but also westward from Edmonton to the town of Dawson Creek. Dawson Creek is a thriving agricultural community and it is also mile zero on the Alaska highway.

subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext: It would be a good place in which to hold this conference.

subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
I quite agree with the member for Skeena that it would be a good place in which to hold the conference. I think that is very magnanimous on his part because it lies in the riding of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe). Incidentally, he and the hon. member for Skeena have almost two-thirds of northern British Columbia in their constituencies.
Let me revert for a moment to mile zero of the Alaska highway at Dawson Creek. During the war the inland access route to Alaska began there and was built northward a distance of approximately 1,200 miles through Canada. About 600 of these miles lie in the province of British Columbia and another 600 miles take you through the Yukon territory as far as the borders of Alaska. From there
June 6, 1966

the Alaska highway runs to the city of Fairbanks. This highway, except for a relatively short piece comprising 36 miles between the town of Dawson Creek and Fort St. John, which lies on the other side of the Peace river, is unpaved. A short stretch of the highway is paved north of Fort St. John but it does not extend very far. What is needed in the opening of the north in order to stimulate not only commercial traffic along that highway but heavy tourist traffic is the continuation of its paving.
About a year or so ago I had the opportunity of discussing this matter with the premier of British Columbia. I asked him what he wanted to see done with the Alaska highway. He said to me: "Institute a federal program of paving the highway as you are its owners and operators and do so on a regular basis of say 100 miles a year extending northward. Turn it over to the province and we will maintain it." That seems to me to be a fair deal and a fair method for getting the Alaska highway paved.
I want to turn for a moment to an alternative suggestion for paving that highway and opening up that section of the north. I refer to a proposal made by two American senators, Senator Mansfield and Senator Metcalf. On January 18, 1964 they introduced in the U.S. Senate Bill S. 2417 to assist Canada on a 50-50 basis in the paving of the Alaska highway. Here are some of the things they would like to see done and which they have written into the provisos of their bill, which is somewhat similar to a private member's bill in this house.
This bill reads in part:
1.	Will provide, without participation of funds herein authorized, all necessary rights of way for the construction of the Alaska highway, which shall forever be held inviolate as a part of the highway for public use;
2.	Will not impose any highway toll-
Note this provision which they would like to see put into the agreement.
-or permit any such toll to be charged, for use by vehicles or persons of any portion of the highway construction under the provisions of this act.
[DOT] (6.40 p.m.)
3.	will not levy or assess, directly or indirectly, any fee, tax, or other charge for the use of said highway by vehicles or persons of the United States that does not apply equally to vehicles or persons of such country;
4.	will grant reciprocal recognition of vehicle registration and drivers licences; and
5.	will provide for year-round maintenance of the highway, including snow removal-
Highways
And so on. Those are the terms of a bill under which they would like to see the Alaska highway paved from Alaska a matter of 1,200 miles to the border. Why should they want to see this done? In the first place,. Alaska is one of the recent states to enter the United States. Alaska fascinates them. If you watch the traffic going through in the summertime you will see people from all over the United States who want to travel that route, one of the most romantic routes in North. America today. The prospect of driving through Alaska during the summer holidays fascinates these people. The ubiquitous Californian, whose station wagons and cars can be found everywhere, hurls himself across the rocks and stones on this road, with stones banging against his car and breaking his windshield. You can walk down the-streets of Dawson Creek at night and look at the cars from the United States parked at the curb.
These cars are covered with dirt and dust after having made the journey from Prince George or having come down the Alaska highway. Their windshields are pitted from the small pebbles that have hit them and some windshields are broken. My wife and I one night walked down the street making a count of how many windshields were broken or pitted. We calculated that approximately 90 per cent of these cars had pitted or broken windshields as a result of rocks being thrown up along the Alaska highway. This was a few years ago. It is no wonder that these people want to see that highway to Alaska paved.
We have a special reason for wanting to see that highway completed. Before it ever reaches Alaska, in which we are really not so greatly interested, there is a cut-off which leads through to Haines and provides access to the sea. This cut-off from the Alaska highway is about 159 miles long and passes through part of the Yukon Territory, part of British Columbia and part of the Alaska panhandle which is United States territory. It is a road that is difficult to keep open in the wintertime because the snow is very heavy but it is an enormously important road because it provides access to the sea at the very top of British Columbia.
It is a very vital matter, therefore, to us to see this road paved so that traffic may move across the northern part of our province to tidewater at Haines. I would prefer to see a federal-provincial conference such as the hon. member has suggested, work out methods for-

June 6, 1966
Highways
the paving of this highway. I would prefer to see the federal government take up the task of paving this highway on a regular basis, mile by mile until the project is completed rather than going to the United States and saying, we will enter into a 50-50 deal with you for the paving of the Alaska highway. In other words, I reject the ideas contained in the Mansfield-Metcalf bill. I suggest we would be far better off in this country if we built our own roads and paid for them. If other nations want access via those roads for purposes of their own, such as to go through the panhandle to Alaska, we should work out through some other kind of arrangement which is satisfactory to them. We should control the building of our own roadways.
I would be happy to see the type of conference suggested by the hon. member. I believe that by building this road ourselves, owning it outright and keeping it in good condition we could go to the United States and say, we are prepared to give you access over the Alaska highway but there are some things that we would like you to settle with us. The first one would be some kind of permanent arrangement about the Alaska panhandle. As hon. members know, this was a deal we got into when we were barely emerging from colonial status at the turn of the century. The negotiators from Great Britain, anxious to go home to the roast beef and ale of England, made a rapid and ready deal with the United States which gave the United States the panhandle which stretches down half the coast of British Columbia. If the 60th parallel were cut through to the sea in this piece of territory which, as it has turned out, has not been so useful to the United States, it would be of inestimable benefit to us. It would give us access to the sea which we greatly need in the northern regions of British Columbia. One of the suggestions I am going to make this evening is that we have such a conference in the future and that we bear in mind that we should be the owners of our own highway system. We should then deal with others on the basis of our complete ownership of that highway system. I believe we should proceed forthwith with the paving of the Alaska highway on a regular, annual basis until it begins to return us solid dividends. I believe, as the hon. member does, that we should be doing everything we can to complete an additional, northern trans-Canada route to serve the growing regions of the north. We should be working toward that objective. I am rather astonished

to hear from my Maritime colleagues how slow the province of Quebec and the Maritimes are in completing the trans-Canada highway for which funds have been available for so long. If they lived in the west, as we do, 3,000 miles from Ottawa, they would realize that the construction of the trans-Canada highway and keeping it in good condition as it is today is a good thing. I know if they drove over it, they would see the reason for completing that highway in the Atlantic provinces.

subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like on this occasion to support the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) in his attempt to indicate to the government that a conference of the nature he has suggested in his resolution should be held, whether it be called a highway conference or simply a road conference. Listening to the parliamentary secretary indicate that there were other programs, the trans-Canada highway program, the roads to resources program and so on, left me with a strong impression that such a conference should be held. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) has indicated that there is a problem in connection with the Alaska highway. He believes a conference of this nature would help solve some of these problems.
The fact that there are problems has been indicated by both the parliamentary secretary and the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I am sure my own province of Saskatchewan could indicate many problems. There may be some provinces that may not require a program of this sort as much as other provinces. There will be some that will not be in a position to undertake construction immediately. However, that should not be a reason for preventing other provinces from progressing.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
The premier of the province of Saskatchewan, having driven the wicked C.C.F. from office, has always told us that the free enterprise government which he heads will try to encourage development. Perhaps it has done that in its own way. However, the roads to resources program is one which will assist the province in its endeavours. It seems to me that the premier of the province of Saskatchewan should be the first to cry out for such a conference.
Last year the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) was asked some questions in the house and said,
June 6, 1966

as reported at page 980 of Hansard for May 6, 1965:
-we have circulated-
The provinces.
-asking for their opinions as to the efficacy of the program.
Surveys have been taken by the department and various departments have been corresponding with the ministers of each province trying to ascertain the need. There is a need, and they must have ascertained the need from the survey which was undertaken. I would have thought that the premier of the province of Saskatchewan might have taken the bull by the horns, so to speak, and put more money into the development of the north, something which in itself would encourage enterprises.
However, Mr. Speaker, since 1963 what do we find? We find a slowdown in roadwork in the north. While the province has asked for extension of the road program for another year, at the same time it has reached the stage where there is no point in rushing. Only a limited amount of money is forthcoming from the federal government, so what is the po;nt of rushing? The federal government has indicated that it will extend this program as well as progress with another program. If it will indicate it is prepared to put aside a certain amount of money and will ask the provinces to work out a program satisfactory to them, I am sure they would be glad to present one to the federal government for its approval or whatever may be necessary.
If this were done the province of Saskatchewan would then know that it would have to match a certain amount. In reply to a question of mine, No. 878, on March 21 it was indicated that the province of Saskatchewan required another $20 million to complete its existing program. We know that under the existing program it is impossible to obtain this amount of money; yet there is the road to Uranium City, the road to Island Falls and the road to Cumberland House. Money is scattered among various projects when it is known it is impossible to complete all of them. However, if the federal government were to indicate that it was quite prepared to put up another $20 million or even $10 million in the case of Saskatchewan, the province would then be able to work out a program.
It may be that the province of Prince Edward Island, for example, might not require such a large amount but would be
Highways
satisfied with another $500,000 to complete its existing program, or it may have other programs in mind. But surely a program of the type indicated by the hon. member for Skeena would help resolve all of these problems.
In the reply to the question which I raised on March 21 I noted that six provinces have asked for an extension. British Columbia, no doubt because of its particular type of problems, asked for an extension of five years for its roads to resources program. Is it fair to the rest of the provinces to wait another five years, some of them perhaps having completed their projects, just because British Columbia has mountain terrain which makes it difficult to complete its roads within the next year or so? This does not seem fair in the case of a program which has worked well.
I am sure there has been support for this program from every corner of the house. I am also sure that a conference at this time would help in the formulation of a program. I do not care who gets the credit for this type of program or who initiates it. Surely we must look at the end result. This might be a wonderful opportunity. I am sure that the idea of roads from igloo to igloo has long passed. I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will agree, and I do not think it necessary to go into that aspect. But when we realize that there are provinces which are prepared to work out programs or to complete existing programs if given further assistance, I think the need for such a conference should be evident to the government.

subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) for bringing his resolution to the attention of the house. The resolution calls for a conference to discuss a national highway building program. I presume this has nothing to do with the trans-Canada highway but rather with a network of access roads in the northern and less developed areas of the nation.
I am all in favour of new highways and access roads. We do not have enough roads in the country to meet the demand of the ever-increasing number of motor vehicles which are using our highways and byways. When we consider that the annual increase in the number of motor vehicles in Canada is of the order of 200,000, the present pace of roadbuilding is nowhere near sufficient to ensure the safety of our motorists. I am not only in favour of the resolution but I would suggest a

June 6, 1966
Highways
national conference in which motor car manufacturers and provincial, municipal and federal representatives would participate.
I also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the present trans-Canada highway be widened to four lanes from coast to coast. At the present time there are four-lane stretches across some parts of Ontario and Quebec and they are indeed a great improvement but unfortunately they do not extend into northern and northwestern Ontario and to other regions of Canada.
I can speak of northwestern Ontario where the worst part of the trans-Canada highway is found. There are stretches between the lakehead and the Manitoba boundary that are really a disgrace to the nation. True, they fall within provincial jurisdiction, but surely when the federal government contributed 90 per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway construction it should also exert some measure of direct control.
May I call it seven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext: The hon. member may have another five minutes.

subtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE ON BUILDING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very much impressed with the idea of having a conference to deal with the very important question of highways, especially with the trans-Canada highway in which I am perhaps more interested. This would provide the opportunity to discuss the construction of access roads to meet the demand which, as I said in my earlier remarks, is increasing at a very fast rate year by year.
I have attended conferences dealing with highways and invariably at every conference the matter of the cost to municipalities, to provinces and to the federal government is raised. This is one of the questions we must meet in some manner. I have suggested at one of these conferences that experts of the highways departments of provincial governments should sit down and try to figure out ways of building highways at less cost.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I was very much impressed when travelling from the city of London, England to the London airport, to see that different sections of the highway were built of different materials. These different materials were used not only to determine the suitability of the substances used, but also to determine the relative costs of the highway. I have not seen anything like it in Canada.

I have suggested, at meetings I have attended, that similar things be done here. There have been favourable discussions, but nothing of a concrete nature has happened. I still wish to make that suggestion, because we must reduce costs.
One finds that public roads cost, per mile, in the neighbourhood of $200,000, $300,000 or $400,000. I agree that some stretches of the trans-Canada highway, especially those last built in southern Ontario, and in some parts of Quebec near Montreal where there are four lanes, are of substantial construction, probably costing as much as I have suggested. However, I suggest that we ought to try to find methods to build highways at reduced costs, because that will result in our building more highways for less money.
I sincerely hope, with respect to the resolution brought forward by the hon. member, that the government and those responsible for these matters will take notice of it, and will convene a conference as suggested, with a view to finding ways and means of coping with the problem.

-this is a very significant resolution. The minister has correctly described it as omnibus in character. Indeed the wide variety of its provisions and their very complex nature has been emphasized by the minister's explanation. But I must say candidly to him, or I would say candidly to him if he were here, that his explanation was exceedingly sketchy, and was indeed more significant and revealing in its omissions than in its elaborations.
The very technical nature of the acts to be amended would indicate that major discussion should await second reading and subsequent committee procedure. But the minister this afternoon indicated that the government intends to group all the proposed amendments in an omnibus bill, rather than introduce separate amending bills for each statute. I object vigorously to this procedure. An omnibus bill such as was adopted in the reorganization of government departments is a most untidy and most confusing legislative process.
I fully adopt what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Kamloops and I reiterate what I urged on two occasions during the discussion of the government reorganization bill. May I put it this way: If in this chamber the government persists in omnibus bills, I hope the other place will exercise proper sober second thought and divide them. I put it specifically to the members of the other place that this is a proper role for a second chamber, if a second chamber must be maintained in our legislative system-and I confess that my views in this respect are very similar to those of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CORRELATION OF VARIOUS PLANS WITH CANADA PENSION PLAN
speechtext: If it is a proper role, let us do it here.

subtopic: CORRELATION OF VARIOUS PLANS WITH CANADA PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
I say, Mr. Chairman, chat one bill amending 15 acts is a travesty upon legislative procedures. It simply ought not to be tolerated in this committee, or in the house at second reading.
Taken as a whole, Mr. Chairman, the superannuation provisions Canada makes for her dedicated public servants are the equal of any country's and compare most favourably with private industry. Only in the treatment of retired public servants who have been caught in the upward trend of prices, for which their pensions make no provision, has the Canadian government been shabby and shoddy. I use these adjectives deliberately because, in relation to this situation, they are
Pensions
mild. I shall have more to say about this, because I firmly believe that we must do two things, and we must do them now. First, we must raise the pensions of those who have retired to the appropriate equivalent of the rates at which they retired and, second, we must build in an escalation clause for the future. I shall return later, in the discussion in committee, to this theme.
I think that the committee will approve of the tidying up operation forecast by the minister this afternoon in respect of the integration of the various superannuation acts and the Canada Pension Plan. The government got itself into an unholy mess by not doing this at the proper time. Does the committee realize that at the present time the government is actually extending to every civil servant a loan, or an accountable advance to the amount of his or her Canada Pension Plan contribution? What a perfectly silly arrangement. This ought to have been looked after at the proper time, long ago. These loans,	or accountable advances
amounted, in the first three months of the year, at March 31, to over $4 million, in accordance with an answer to a question of mine which was brought down in the house this afternoon.
As the law stands, every civil servant must contribute the full superannuation rate of 5 per cent or 6J per cent, as the case may be, plus-and I emphasize this-the full Canada Pension Plan contributions. This bill presumably cancels out these loans, affecting a bookkeeping transfer as between the superannuation funds and the Canada Pension Plan. If ever I saw an illustration of untidy, slovenly, disjointed administration, it is in the way the government has handled this whole matter.

subtopic: CORRELATION OF VARIOUS PLANS WITH CANADA PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
How would the hon. member have done it?
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)

subtopic: CORRELATION OF VARIOUS PLANS WITH CANADA PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
Done it neatly at the proper time by legislative action, as it ought to have been done. It is the dilatoriness of this government-always postponing something to another day-which has led to this situation.
A very large number of complaints have reached me about the practice of requiring that Canada Pension Plan deductions be taken from salary increases retroactively made. The result has been to levy deductions upon salaries actually earned in 1965 before the plan came into effect. It seems to me this is unwarranted and I would ask the minister to

June 6, 1966
Pensions
deal with this question in the course of his reply. According to a question of mine which was answered this afternoon and which, presumably, will appear in Hansard tomorrow the sum of $210,000 was collected in 1966 from civil servants in respect of salary earned in 1965, before the Canada Pension Plan came into effect.
Before this bill passes the house we shall want to be assured of certain things. I shall list them. First, that the integration of the Canada Pension Plan and the superannuation acts will not be detrimental to any public servants and will be more favourable to some. Second, that the basic principles of the superannuation acts are not violated or substantially altered. As I have said, the superannuation acts are sound. Personally, I believe the benefits available under the Public Service Superannuation Act should be placed upon the basis of a five-year average. They should never have been related to a ten-year average, as was done by hon. gentlemen opposite. Many of the hardships suffered by retired civil servants are the result of that ill-advised action in establishing a ten-year average. The best I was able to achieve when the act was last revised was to have the period dropped back to a six-year average. I plead today with the minister to recognize that in these times of rapidly shifting costs and frequent changes in salary levels, the least he could do would be to include a five-year average in the act.
In the third place we want an assurance that an attempt will be made to build into the superannuation acts an escalation principle. This has been accepted as a matter of policy by the government in relation to the Canada Pension Plan. Introduced into the superannuation acts it would become a technique for avoiding the hardships and injustices which have confronted so many retired civil servants. And it would set a standard for industry which would be most desirable.
Now in respect to certain injustices-the minister called them anomalies-which have arisen in the administration of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the hon. gentleman has indicated that the bill will seek authority to deal with these by regulation or by orders in council.
I object as vigorously as I can to this technique of bypassing parliament. If the new procedures in the mind of the government can be outlined by regulation, or in an order in council, they can be set forth in the statute itself. The injustices are recognized. The time

to cure them is now, openly in this chamber, not in some back room. What evidence do we have that the government really intends to take action on this matter, one which has been hanging fire for a long time, when they conceal from this house what they propose to do?
The first problem I wish to raise concerns pensioned officers of the armed forces who are employed in the civil service. The existing provisions of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act relating to receipt of pensions while employed in the civil service are out of date and harshly unjust. Under these provisions a retired officer, warrant officer or chief petty officer entitled to a pension or annuity may receive, when subsequently employed in the civil service, only that part of his pension or annuity which, when added to his civil service pay, does not exceed his pay on retirement or the current pay in effect for the rank he held at the time of his retirement, whichever is greater.
This provision has had two deleterious effects. It has deprived the civil service of the services of highly trained and skilled officers who might have made a further major contribution to the public well-being. Second, it has brought injustice and hardship to those retired officers who, despite this discrimination, have entered federal employment. Many of them are my friends. I admire their personal loyalty as much as I deprecate the policy which deprives them of fair remuneration to which they are entitled.
The minister gave us no inkling of how he proposed to deal with this matter. He seeks a blank cheque to deal with it behind closed doors, by regulation. That is not good enough. This committee is entitled to be told what is planned with respect to a matter about which the government has been stalling-deliberately stalling-for months and months. If a remedy can be found by regulation it can be found by statute, in which case this chamber and all those persons who are affected will know what is proposed and can assess whether or not the solution is just and equitable. If we do not learn now what the government proposes it may be months, even years, before this issue is settled. I want an answer from the minister now, before this legislation passes. I do not wish to give the government a blank cheque in respect to this matter.
I turn now to the pension status of persons who enlisted in the armed forces during the war and continued to serve after the war
June 6, 1966

ended. The interpretation of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act has led to major discrimination and the minister has given no indication of the nature of his proposals.
The problem is this: the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act of 1959 makes eligibility for annuity dependant upon whether the contributor served in the armed forces for certain minimum periods. This was based upon the concept that these minimum periods of entitlement should be in the regular or permanent forces in order to qualify the contributor for pension. Active service during world war II by a person who was not a member of the forces as defined in the act does not count in this qualifying period, but once the qualifying period is satisfied the active service can be counted as pensionable service in the benefit formula.
Where there is a 25-year requirement and an officer wants to retire before normal retirement age, his war service has been totally eliminated from calculation. In my view, this is a genuine injustice-a real discrimination and must be rectified-and the place to rectify this is in the statute, not by regulation or order in council. I want the minister's answer tonight-not at some vague and indefinite date in the equally vague future.
One particular case of major injustice I wish to present without mentioning names, but arising out of the rule that a widow more than 25 years younger than her deceased husband is not entitled to pension. Protection against death-bed marriages is, of course, necessary, but some discretion ought to be provided to deal with harsh and unjust cases. In the particular case to which I refer a lieutenant colonel, at age 49, married a young woman of 22. It was a happy and productive marriage which lasted for 31 years, until the lieutenant colonel died at the age of 80. His widow is 26 years and four months younger than her deceased husband, and after 31 years of marriage she is deprived of pension.
I have given the Minister of Finance and the Associate Minister of National Defence full particulars, but I fear the bill to be founded on this resolution will not enable justice to be done in this particular case. If it does not, I shall have to deal with this matter, in detail, in committee.
Finally, sir, a brief word about pension increases for retired public servants, members of the R.C.M.P. and armed forces. I would have hoped that the phrase "amendments of a general nature in connection with the administration of those acts" in the last
Pensions
sentence of this resolution could be given real meaning by immediate and decisive action to raise these pensions. Since the minister has been silent, apparently it does not. I am deeply disappointed.
My views are well known. I have argued them in this house and outside on many occasions. It was an indiscreet speech of mine in 1957-deliberately indiscreet-which made it certain that readjustments would be achieved by the former government in 1958. Frankly, I am appalled by the adamant attitude of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister on this issue. I say to them both that I believe the will of this parliament is that justice and equity be done to the retired servants of the crown, and they cannot long stand in the way of that will. Both of them are former civil servants and ought to understand better the principles involved.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Personally I believe the Public Service Superannuation Act and other acts should have now a built-in escalation clause, and the contribution should reflect this. I will refer to this further on second reading and in committee. But this does not help the retired civil servants who now are enduring major hardships because due to the failures of the government, the dollar value of their pensions has declined so steeply.
My views are set forth as neatly as I could put them in resolution No. 28 which I introduced and which has been on the order paper since January 20. Because I fear it will not be reached at this session of parliament, I should like to read it:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give the earliest possible consideration to the advisability of adjusting upwards the pensions of superannuated public servants and of superannuated members of the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to take appropriate account of increases in the cost of living, increases in salary levels and other relevant factors occurring since the rates of pension of such persons were determined.
This only I add: In other countries, notably Great Britain and the United States, precisely this has been done. The government of the right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert established a precedent in Canada, and all that needs to be done is to bring that legislation up to date. The right hon. gentleman for Prince Albert has been the best practical friend the superannuated civil servants have ever had, and I urge respectfully but firmly upon the present Prime Minister emulation of his example. I appeal to the Minister of

June 6. 1966
Pensions
Finance and the Prime Minister for justice now for those who have served Canada well.
Thank you.

subtopic: CORRELATION OF VARIOUS PLANS WITH CANADA PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, because of the time limitation we are under at this stage of debate, because of the complex nature of this piece of legislation, and also because of the limited number of details we have been given, it will not be possible to deal with it in full at this time. However, this is a most important piece of legislation and I trust ample time will be provided on second reading and in committee of the whole for us to go into this bill in the manner it deserves.
This piece of legislation does two main things. In the first place it brings before us the government's policy concerning integration of the various government pension plans with the Canada Pension Plan. That is a very simple statement when one makes it in one sentence; but when he realizes the number of government pension plans and the complexity *of the formula which has been worked out, it becomes clear that there is a lot more to it than can be put in one simple sentence. The other main purpose of this legislation is to make a number of general amendments to pension legislation, and apparently this is being done in this way because the subject matter of government pensions is before the house at this time.
With regard to the policy concerning integration I should like to say that, even though I may be a voice crying in the wilderness and even though we may have to accept this legislation because the representatives of the public servants-I am told-agree to it, I still am in disagreement with it. I disagree with the government's policy, but not for the reasons advanced by the hon. member for Carleton. I disagree with it because it is my view that complete integration-and that is what the government's policy is-denies one of the main purposes for which the Canada Pension Plan was brought in.
As I see it, the Canada Pension Plan had two main purposes. On the one hand it was *designed to provide a basic pension for all wage earners in this country, having in mind in particular those who previously had no pension plan whatsoever. The other purpose [DOT]of the Canada Pension Plan, however, was to improve the pension position of those who already had some pension arrangements. In other words, the second purpose was to add to the pension possibilities many of our people already had. I quite recognize there are pensions which are so good that no addition, no

supplement, to them really is necessary; but most pensions in this country are not in that category.
As time goes on, as living costs go up and as living standards go up, we are learning that there are more and more people on pensions which they thought were going to be adequate, and which they now find are not going to be adequate. As a result of all this we are learning there is a need for supplementation to most pensions. Therefore one of the reasons I was glad to support the Canada Pension Plan-and I was a strong supporter of it from start to finish-was that it provided an additional pension for those who already had pension arrangements and as well provided pensions for those who had not.
However, when under the name of integration you take away from the pension arrangement you already have all or practically all of what you are going to get under the Canada Pension Plan, then you have made no improvement for those persons who already had some pension arrangement. I know that a happy medium has to be found, or a line has to be drawn somewhere, but in my view the government's action in saying, in so far as its employees are concerned, that they are to get practically no improvement as a result of coming under the Canada Pension Plan, is a denial of one of the main purposes of the Canada Pension Plan. This also is a case of giving a very poor lead to private employers in this country.
I know the argument used is that 5 per cent and 64 per cent are high contribution rates and that those who pay these contributions do not want to pay any more. When those same people retire on their pensions they will wish they had a little more and that they had had the opportunity to pay a little more, even 1.8 per cent; but when the government lays down as a policy a complete integration that takes away the benefit which the Canada Pension Plan would have provided, private employers across the country use that as an excuse. Many of them are doing the same thing, even in respect of pensions where the contribution rates are lower than those in the government service and where the pension benefits are much lower.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
I contend therefore that this principle of what amounts to almost complete integration is, as I say, a denial of benefits and rights to public servants that they might have enjoyed, and it is also a very poor lead to private employers.
June 6, 1966

In all of this I am talking about the government's legislation as though it took away everything by complete integration, but I know that it does not go that far. There are a few instances where there is a marginal improvement as a result of which an employee will pay a total amount that is exactly the same as he would have paid, but will get a little more in the end. The main reason he will get a little more is that, dollar for dollar, money put into the Canada pension plan buys a better pension than money put into the public service superannuation fund. This is also true with respect to many private pension plans. I recognize the fact that there is marginal improvement and that some employees will get a little bit more, but that does not detract from the basic principle that this legislation, which will leave the total amount that civil servants are paying exactly the same, guarantees only that the benefits will not drop.
In my view it would have been better to work out a principle of integration that would give a little here and would give a little there. Perhaps the total contribution could have been increased by one half of one per cent or by one full percentage point. That is the kind of thing that I think would have been more acceptable in the long run to our public servants, and would have provided a better lead to employers across the country. We will be able to go into these things in greater detail when we reach second reading or committee stage, but I want to indicate at this point why I think we are being taken down a path on which we should not be travelling.
The minister this afternoon referred a number of times to this legislation as implementing recommendations of the joint committee on the Canada Pension Plan. While there may be many of those recommendations which will be implemented, surely the one that he is talking about when he refers to integration is the one which reads:
There should be scope for further benefits under private pension plans for those in a position to afford them and integration of private pension plans with the Canada Pension Plan should be a matter of consultation between employers and employees.
In other words, we in the committee recognized that there would be integration. But, we had before us many bodies, particularly of employees who were concerned that the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan would be taken away from them under the cloak of
Pensions
integration. They asked us to support them in the suggestion that any such arrangements should be a matter of consultation. What kind of consultation there has been in this instance I do not know, but I do know that in private business there has been far too many unilateral decisions by the employers who simply say to the employees that they are going to get this benefit from the Canada Pension Plan, so half or all of what they would get under the old plan will be taken away; and they have suggested they are justified in taking this action because the federal government is doing the same thing. That is my view of the situation; but we will cover it in detail when we reach the committee stage of the debate.
I welcome the announcement that the legislation will be worded in such a way that something will be done about the armed service and the R.C.M.P., as we recommended in the report of the joint committee on the Canada Pension Plan. The point raised by the hon. member for Carleton, that this sort of thing should be spelled out in the legislation rather than just being made a subject of regulation by order in council, was well taken. I welcome also the decision that among the things to be done in a general way regarding the pension plans of the government there will be an improvement in the supplementary death benefit provided for civil servants. The $5,000 level that is in the act at the present time has become an inadequate amount, and the suggested change is all to the good.
I also welcome the suggestion that something is going to be done for defence personnel, particularly those referred to by the hon. member for Carleton, who have wartime service but so far have not been able to count that service for pension purposes if they choose to retire early. I trust this change is included in the legislation, because on two or three occasions I have asked about it and the Associate Minister of National Defence has indicated to me across the floor of the house that it would be included in this omnibus legislation now before us. I will have to wait until I see the legislation before I can decide whether it is satisfactory just to have this provided for as a regulation or whether it should be included by actual legislation in the statute itself.
I should like to say now a few words about the things that in my view certainly ought to be included in this legislation, but concerning which so far there is no evidence that they

June 6, 1966
Pensions
will be. One of the points that civil service organizations and organizations of retired civil servants have been making is the need for altering, indeed improving, the formula under which pensions of widows of civil servants are calculated. The hon. member for Carleton referred to one specific situation, namely the age differential that is included in the legislation. There is also a question in respect of the formula under which the amounts of widows' pensions are calculated.
It has been a contention among civil servants, and particularly retired civil servants, that something should be done about this formula by this legislation. Since this resolution does state that there can be amendments of a general nature, I hope that there will be a change, in the formula under which the pensions of widows of civil servants are calculated.
This leads me, so far as this limited period of time is concerned, to the one remaining point about which I want to speak. This is a point to which the member for Carleton directed the major and warmest part of his remarks, and I join him in that warmth. I think it is an utter disgrace that this government goes on, and on, and on, constantly refusing to make any improvements in the pensions of civil servants already retired. The excuses we are given time after time just do not stand up or hold water. These excuses carry less weight and less conviction than ever, now that this goverment has recognized the need for escalators in pension legislation.
In the Old Age Security Act there has been written an escalator provision that will provide for a possible increase of 75 cents or $1.50 per month, from year to year. If we are around long enough we may get old age pensions up to $100 per month, but it will take a long time. At least the principle has been accepted, that even though a pension has been put into pay, conditions change and pensions need to be increased. An escalator that applies after a pension is put into pay applies not only to the Old Age Security Act but also to the Canada Pension Plan. Whatever pension a person will get when he retires on the Canada Pension Plan is subject to an increase if the cost of living goes up in subsequent years.
In addition to that, there has been built into the Canada Pension Plan an escalator which increases the potential value of a contributor's pension during the years he is working and contributing to the plan. The

escalator which operates while the contributor is working is geared to the wage index. In other words, it is geared to an increase in productivity and to the fact that the standard of living goes up.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
If that principle has been accepted, and I give the government credit for it, then I ask: Why should it stop where it does? These people we are talking about, retired civil servants, are the retired employees of the people of Canada. They worked for all of us. They worked for this government. If their pensions are low, it is for reasons beyond their control. I submit that it is the height of inhumanity, it is callousness in the extreme, for the government to go on saying to these people, "We can raise other people's pensions; we can raise other people's salaries; we can build escalators into other pension plans, but yours is a contractual arrangement and we can do nothing at all about it."
Talking about what other employers do is beside the point. The government's responsibility in this matter is not only that of government, which it has to all our people, but it also has its responsibility as an employer. I submit that at this time when the government has in effect opened up the Public Service Superannuation Act, has admitted that some benefits have to be raised, such as the supplemental death benefit, which is being raised from $5,000 to a higher figure, when it recognizes that such changes and improvements have to be made, it just is not acceptable for us to be asked to pass this bill without doing something for the civil servants already retired, and for their widows.
The hon. member for Carleton pointed out that this has been done in other jurisdictions, the United States and the United Kingdom for example, that it has been done by a number of provinces in this country-it has been done in this very province of Ontario for the teachers-that it has been done in certain municipalities, for example in my own city of Winnipeg, namely the raising of pensions of people already retired. It was also done by the parliament of Canada during the years when the present right hon. member for Prince Albert was prime minister of this country. If it has been done in so many areas, it is a principle that can be followed, and I urge that it be done while we have this legislation before us.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, this is an important piece of legislation which covers two
June 6. 1S66

main things, how we handle integration and incidental changes in our pensions generally.
I will have something to say about integration when we reach second reading of the bill and committee of the whole, unless perchance the government decides to send the bill to a special committee where people can appear and we can go into the bill more thoroughly.
I have stated my views. We may have to accept the bill as it is; but I deeply and bitterly regret that when the government has brought in such a good piece of legislation as the Canada Pension Plan it should by its own lead encourage private employers to take the same kind of step, with the result that many people are denied the improvements they might otherwise have had. On the other side of the ledger are the incidental improvements being made to our various pieces of pension legislation, and I welcome the fact that some changes that needed to be made are being made; and so far as the minister indicated them to us, they are good.
But what is the matter with the minister, what is the matter with the government, opening up this issue of the Public Service Superannuation Act, knowing how serious this matter is, knowing how many hundreds of letters come to the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and members of parliament day after day, week after week, and then saying that we must put this legislation through without doing anything for our retired civil servants? I can tell the minister that if provision for these people is not made in the legislation he will hear more about it, not only from me but from a good many other members of this house, for all of us want to do the right thing by our retired civil servants.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words at this stage of the resolution. We shall certainly have more to say on second reading, in view of the fact that the province of Quebec constitutes a special case since it has its own pension scheme.
This resolution is to introduce:
A measure to be known as the Canada Assistance Plan, to establish a program for sharing with the provinces in the cost of assistance.
As far as we in Quebec are concerned, we realize that when the federal government gives a benefit, it necessarily takes more in return. That is where our problem arises in Quebec, where we have our own pension
Pensions
plan, our own public assistance program, our pensions for the blind and for assistance to the disabled.
I believe that at this stage of discussion in committee the specific case of the province of Quebec will have to be considered. We should no longer have to pay administration costs. In fact, I believe that if the federal government intrudes further into such social assistance programs, it will necessarily have to tax us.
To my mind, what we have to discuss is this: The federal government must cease to tax the province of Quebec in order to pay us back. I have said it previously in the house, Mr. Chairman, we are old enough to levy our own taxes. We have no need of the federal government to levy taxes in areas that belong to us, that are totally within provincial jurisdiction.
I cannot understand the federal government not wanting to discuss this specific case. The Minister of National Revenue should discuss with the provincial authorities rather than levying a tax and paying back part of it to the province of Quebec.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
The province of Quebec should be given back a percentage of taxes equivalent to the majority help which will be given to the other provinces since they accept that national plan. The province of Quebec does not want to join in the national program because it has adopted its own pension plan and we support it. As far as the social assistance plan is concerned, once again the federal government helps the province of Quebec, but it is not the kind of help which we want.
We are asking the federal government to stop giving us those amounts and to give us the equivalent instead, that is a percentage of our taxation rights until we are given them in full once and for all. Twenty years ago the federal government took over the property tax from the province of Quebec and it is giving it back to us bit by bit. It should give us back once and for all our taxation fields and our property tax. We feel that those three taxation fields, namely personal income tax, corporation income tax and succession duties, belong by right to the provinces; they should be given back to them and the government should stop coming to the province of Quebec to get $10 and give it back $3. It is precisely against that attitude that we will fight when this bill is considered. We are not against other provinces who want to walk together.

June 6. 1966
Pensions
Quebec has clearly indicated its stand in that field, as well as in the fields of health, agriculture, forestry, which come under the provinces. The provinces should be left free once and for all to administer them, especially Quebec whose cause I want to plead here; the door should be thrown wide open to agreements in order to avoid that double administration. It seems to me that this would help the federal government while giving much more to the province; that would also prevent taxes from going back and forth. One knows that taxes are a little like water flowing in a river; a little is always lost along the way, so that finally it is found that if it is posible to recover 30 per cent of the taxes which were taken from us, that is all that we can recover.
Mr. Chairman, I just want to warn the house that we will watch this bill closely not only at the committee stage but also on second reading. We will certainly ask that a percentage of the taxes which belong to us be given back to us instead of sums of money; thus we will be able to continue to pay the costs of our own health insurance plans, as we are doing right now for our pension plan, until we have the other programs which also belong to us, as the Quebec minister of health requested recently. Besides, I think that the government which was elected yesterday will ask for it even more vigorously; I hope that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) will understand the reason why we are fighting; it is simply that we want to keep in Quebec what belongs to us.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to say a few words in support of the resolution that is now before the committee. I also want to express my dissatisfaction with the way in which this particular measure has been brought before the house. It has been referred to as an omnibus resolution, and I suppose the bill will follow along the same line. I think the nature of this resolution is unfortunate. It is confusing and illogical, and I think it is almost impossible to enter into a logical debate on the measure as it is presently brought before us.
I rise mainly to add my voice of protest against the failure of the government to make any adequate provision for retired civil servants. Throughout the past several years this matter has been raised in the house on many occasions, not only in debates in the house but also in the private members' hour. It has been raised as well in the question period on

orders of the day, and I was very disappointed the other day when, I believe it was the Prime Minister, in reply to a question that was posed to him stated that no consideration was being given to bringing in at this time a measure to increase the pensions of the superannuated civil servants.
It is a matter of wonderment to many of us and to many people across this country that the government can find millions of dollars for this, that, and the other purpose; they can find hundreds of millions of dollars for other projects; but when it comes to a matter of superannuated civil servants, old age pensioners and others, there is just not enough money to give these people a few extra dollars a month to help them meet the cost of living.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that the people across the country are wondering where the priorities are placed and what the government is thinking of in refusing to make provision for our own people when, as I say, millions of dollars are being provided for operations and for services overseas. We are not objecting to them; we believe in them; but we also believe we must make provision for these people who are living in our midst and who are living on the borderline of poverty. It is not their fault that the cost of living is increasing. In some respects it is owing to government policies that are adopted and implemented, and because of other situations that have developed. I say it is not the fault of these people that the cost of living is increasing, and yet they are caught in the squeeze.
The letters we receive from some of these people are pathetic in the extreme. They point out the fact that when they go to buy their groceries each week they find their dollar buys a little less; it is shrinking. They are trying to get by on a diet that is far from satisfactory and adequate to maintain their health and strength.
This was the main purpose for which I rose to participate briefly in this debate. I wish to challenge the government once again to reassess its position in regard to superannuated civil servants, those who are unable to get by and make some provision to live out their days, not in a position of luxury but with sufficient means to maintain themselves with some degree of comfort and security.
Now, Mr. Chairman, reference has been made to the purpose of this particular resolution to effect the correlation of the various public service pension plans with the Canada Pension Plan. This was a matter of concern when the pension plan was first introduced. It
June 6. 1966

has been a matter of concern ever since that time. Those who have other types of pension and have made provision for their own needs through other pension plans have wondered just how they are going to fit into the over-all Canada Pension Plan. We realize that some of these changes are necessary and that it is necessary that they be correlated.
Of course, if the civil service organizations are satisfied this is the best way to accomplish the objective, then we have no objection to it. While I do criticize the government on one or two points, yet I recognize the importance of the resolution that is before us. This is the extent of my remarks at this particular stage.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to support this resolution I wish to state frankly that I do wish it went further than it does at the present time. This resolution covers five specific acts: the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, the Diplomatic Service (Special) Superannuation Act and the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways Employees' Provident Act. We are told that it is to provide for a deduction in the contributions required to be paid under those acts as a result of the implementation of the Canada Pension Plan and for the correlation of the pensions or annuities payable under those acts with the pensions payable under the Canada Pension Plan.
I am a strong believer in setting an example rather than in telling other people what they should do. Actions speak louder than words in my book, and I believe in the books of most Canadians. I would like to ask the government why, if they have an omnibus clause-and I am not objecting to such a resolution covering five acts-they could not also have included a sixth act for action at this time, namely Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, under which all the members of parliament are beneficiaries.
The minister, in introducing the resolution this afternoon, stated that there are 15 or 20 acts which need to be changed because of the coming into force of the Canada Pension Plan. Later on in his remarks he stated that a method of integration had been perfected during the past few months.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
Now, the riding which has done me the honour of sending me to Ottawa in three
Pensions
consecutive elections contains five municipalities, and those municipalities are contained within metropolitan Toronto. My riding is the only riding in the Toronto area which has such a large number of municipalities making up the one riding. Some of the metropolitan Toronto ridings have as many as three municipalities in them, but York-Humber has five. The constituency includes the town of Weston, the village of Swansea, the town of Mimico, part of the township of Etobicoke and part of the township of York. Then, over and above that, we have the metropolitan Toronto government. The net result is that in this riding of York-Humber there are residents who are covered by the pension plans of six different municipal councils.
I have supported the Canada Pension Plan from the embryonic stage. I agree it may only be a first step and that there should be further steps before we are through with this measure, but the people of Canada will be assured of decent pensions in the future. The present Canada Pension Plan is a terrific first step. When the plan was announced these municipal governments to which I have alluded were faced with the question, should they stack their present municipal pensions on the Canada Pension, or should they integrate? Interestingly enough, of the six municipal councils, three of them decided to integrate and three decided to stack. Immediately I had constituents coming to me and asking if the federal government could not force all the municipal councils to stack. It was apparent of course that these municipal employees-I will call them state employees-wanted the Canada Pension Plan and the municipal pension plan stacked, because in that way the municipal taxpayer would be contributing to the municipal plan as well as the municipal employee, and under the Canada Pension Plan the Canadian taxpayer would be contributing to the plan as well as the municipal employee. These people would be getting two contributions from the Canadian taxpayers and the benefits would be payable to one employee when the age of pension was reached.
I felt very strongly, and still do, that where an employee is being paid by a municipal government, provincial government or federal government, his pension plans should be integrated. I do not believe for one moment that the taxpayers should be asked to pay into pension plans twice which are going to be of benefit ultimately to one individual pensioner. I do believe that this omnibus resolution-I

June 6, 1966
Pensions
am not using the expression in a derogatory sense although some people consider it a bad feature-should have included the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act. When I received my May remuneration, as all members of parliament did at the end of the month, there was attached to the cheque a statement of earnings and deductions for the month of May. A very interesting situation hits you right between the eyes when you look at that statement. We, as members of parliament, are having our pension plans stacked.
How can we legislate at this time for a couple of hundred thousand public employees under these five acts, the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, the Diplomatic Service (Special) Superannuation Act and the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways Employees' Provident Act, in order to integrate the Canadian Pension Plan with their present plans while we continue to have our own plans stacked? It is all right to say that there are 15 or 20 acts which need to be changed in view of the advent of the Canada Pension Plan. I pointed out on Friday afternoon that we have had four promises in four consecutive Speeches from the Throne that there are going to be changes in the Canadian Citizenship Act, but the changes have not been made yet. We tell the people we are going to change the terms of the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act some day. I think the public would appreciate it a great deal more if the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act were integrated with the Canada Pension Plan at this time when we are integrating these other five plans. Then the public would see that we mean to treat ourselves in exactly the same way as we are endeavouring to legislate for the employees of the federal government.
If you look at your May cheque, you will find a deduction of $60 for the House of Commons pension. Then you will find the deduction of $10.80 for the Canada Pension Plan. The federal government, of course, is contributing to both of these plans, and each one of us is the individual beneficiary. The taxpayers are contributing twice. I believe that when we are integrating plans for the people covered by the five acts enumerated in the resolution we would have been in a much

stronger position if the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act had been included in the resolution. I ask that the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act be put into the bill when it is brought forward here, because that is a vital and necessary improvement. Let us not put ourselves in the position of not paying any attention to what the cabinet is doing under the five acts, but just integrate these acts in the thought that some day in the future we will amend the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act. Let us show we mean it and amend the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act at this time as well.

speechtext:
I think the resolution before us will be a great disappointment to a great number of Canadians who had expected that in the housekeeping operations of the government revolving around the civil servants, we would be dealing with some of the issues that were raised so eloquently earlier this evening by the hon. member for Carleton, supported by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others who took part in the debate. I cast about for a phrase to sum up the resolution we are now considering. At one point I considered that it might be described as a good housekeeping resolution that would mean the melding of the operations of the Canada Pension Plan with these other plans that are being considered. However, I have come to the conclusion it is a minimum housekeeping operation dealing with the cold facts and figures that chartered accountants might present concerning the operation of these pension plans, with little thought to the needs of the people who are supposed to be benefited.
All of us have received submissions from groups of civil servants, especially the Civil Service Federation of Canada, whose president Mr. C. A. Edwards, on March 24 of this year wrote the following:
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
It Is a fact that the cost of living has increased 40 per cent in the past 15 years, over 20 per cent in the past 10 years, and approximately 10 per cent in the past five years. feel that I cannot let this opportunity pass without saying a few words about this resolution. We have all heard from organizations of superannuated civil servants across the country, communications from many of which have been read during the course of this debate. Tonight I want to take a few minutes to examine two cases, to point out how this matter works in the lives of people concerned.
I have noticed that when one comes to the House of Commons in Ottawa, unless great care is exercised one is apt to see people as statistics and figures in columns, and to forget that they are flesh and blood, capable of suffering, and of having feelings, as we all have in the chamber. For the most part speaking generally these people are a great deal less cushioned against the difficulties and hardships of living than we are. I am talking of those superannuated civil servants who have been writing to us from across the country. How does all this work out in the lives of these people?
Pensions
I want to take two examples, both from British Columbia. One is a man who worked as a civil servant for many years in one government department, and who was superannuated recently. Of course his pension does not meet the cost of living today, nor the standard of living which is rising through the years. This man found on retirement that he could not make ends meet for himself and his wife. In desperation he looked around for a job. It might have been expected that a grateful country would see that his pension would keep him in reasonable comfort for the rest of his life. Instead of that, on retirement he was forced to look for work. As he went around he found himself in competition with younger people, and he found it impossible to get any work of any kind that would bring him in an income. At last he went to the Department of Public Works hoping that the government would give him casual employment, so that he might work on and off. Instead the door was closed in his face, and he was told that the department would not hire anybody over retirement age. So, here is a man and his wife having to get along on a miserable pittance of a pension in the face of rising living costs.
This man feels bitterly that he has been let down, that he gave his best to the country. His record as a civil servant was good. He feels, now that other people have the Canada Pension Plan, and are laying by for their old age in a much better way than formerly, that he has been let down in a very ungrateful way by the country to which he gave his services.
Here is another case. A letter was written to me by a friend of the woman in question. The letter says:
I felt you would be outstandingly sympathetic to a lovely gentle widow-a family friend. We have watched her struggle to maintain a good appearance and an adequate living on the pittance she receives from our federal government.
Her husband retired in 1941 from the office of the District Director of Postal Services on account of a heart condition. He had been employed for more than thirty-three years at that time by the civil service. He died in June 1957 of cancer after a long painful illness through which they asked for and received no assistance. Both have and had a great Scotch pride of independence.
His wife carried on working as a relief in the local post office till veterans replaced her. Now she is forced to exist on $62.88 (sixty-two dollars and eighty-eight cents). She has maintained an old beach cottage in White Rock making it look charming with her care.
[DOT] (8.30 p.m.)
She pays $157.29 taxes, fuel and light comes to $17 (used sparingly) telephone $3.25, water $3 per month.

June 6, 1966

We have worries of "what if the house foundations gave way? What if she needed health and dental care?"
It truly hurts us to think that a widow of one of our former Canadian servants is treated so very shabbily.
She asks me what can be done to help this widow at this stage of life-this widow who had bravely seen her husband through a painful illness, cancer, met the medical costs as best she could, filled in at the local post office, and finally been forced to eke out an existence.
These are the things we should consider today before we consider benefits for those who are in better circumstances. Everyone needs pension plans, but we should not throw on the scrap heap those others who have given their best to their country. To do so would be to show ingratitude and insensitivity; it would certainly be showing that we are not competent to look after the needs of the people who live in this country.
These retired civil servants do not have eternity in which to wait. Most of us here in this group feel that if we wait long enough the benefits which we are seeking for our fellow Canadians will be provided. We know from experience that after 30 years or so the things for which we are fighting will be made effective. But these superannuated people are for the most part, elderly. Unless something can be done for them now they will pass their late years feeling they have been cheated and treated unfairly by a country to which they have given years of service and the best that is in them.
I strongly urge that something be done without delay to help these superannuated people. Surely it will not involve a major expense. This is unfinished business of a most urgent kind and I certainly join with the hon. member who preceded me in his plea that before we concern ourselves with the pensions of members of parliament and other well situated people we should consider those who are virtually penniless at this time, unless the government comes to their aid.
