Mr. Chairman, I am
prompted to say a few words particularly with reference to the statement the minister made that the retired civil servants will not be affected in any way by this legislation. The fact is that retired civil servants feel they have an interest and a stake in the federal Civil Service Superannuation Act and in the fund that is established by this act. Whether rightly or wrongly, the fact is that they have an interest in the fund. They are afraid and concerned that any amendment to the Civil Service Superannuation Act might affect their entitlement under the fund, a fund which was created by the Public Service Superannuation Act.
I know the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Revenue have written to them and have said that in no way will their entitlement under this act be affected by any integration of the Public Service Superannuation Act with the Canada Pension Plan. However, many doubts have been raised in the minds of retired civil servants by the passage of the Canada Pension Plan. Over the years civil servants have felt their rights are protected under the Public Service Superannuation Act by virtue of the fact that it is an actuarially sound funded plan. But then along comes the Canada Pension Plan, a major contributory pension plan, which affects people who retire in the future. The

government says, that this major plan, which affects the pensions of future Canadians is not based on an actuarially funded plan. Immediately the question arises in the minds of retired public servants: If the Canada Pension Plan is not based on a funded basis, why should ours be?-keeping in mind the fact that the vast majority of retired civil servants are living under severely handicapped conditions by virtue of the fact that their pension is fixed whereas the cost of living rises? So, in the every day events these people say: Why should our pension be fixed; is there no responsibility on the part of the government toward its employees?
These same civil servants have in mind that in 1959 the previous government of this country passed an Act, the federal Civil Service Superannuation Adjustment Act, which did adjust the pensions of a large number of retired civil servants. So the fact is that these retired civil servants are justly concerned in respect of how their position is affected by the integration of the Public Service Superannuation Act with the Canada Pension Plan. I think the only way in which these people can be satisfied is by their having an opportunity to present their case to representatives of the House of Commons. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that this resolution No. 51, at the appropriate stage, should be referred to a special or standing committee.
The Canada Pension Plan is a very complicated piece of legislation. It was referred to a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons. Speaking from memory, I believe that committee held 51 sittings. I think there were something in the order of 30 briefs presented to it. It was a complicated piece of legislation.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
In order to understand integration of the P.S.S.A. and other pension schemes with the Canada Pension Plan, we must clearly understand not only the Canada Pension Plan but the other acts which must be amended in order to complete this integration. If it was necessary, and certainly it was, to submit the proposed Canada pension to a committee then even more so is it necessary to submit to a committee the proposal to integrate these other pension plans with the Canada Pension Plan.
At this stage the minister cannot, of course, describe in any detail the proposal for integration of these plans, but various statements have been made by him and by others as to
June 6, 1966

the general proposals. Assuming that these proposals will be incorporated in the bill, which the minister will in due course present, I predict there will be grave anomalies disclosed when integration is attempted.
I predict that many civil servants will find themselves in the fortunate position of having an increase after the proposed integration of something like 25 per cent in their pensions, whereas other civil servants will find that there will be no increase. More power to those who receive 25 per cent more, but how will this fact sit with those who receive no increase whatsoever? Furthermore, I predict that if the bill to be introduced by the minister conforms to the statements he has made up to date, we will find that in certain cases potential widows of civil servants yet to be retired will receive pensions larger than the earnings of their husbands. All the more power to those widows; but how will this fact sit with other Canadians, and particularly those who are now widows of civil servants who receive nothing whatsoever from either the public service superannuation fund or the Canada Pension Plan.
I predict that when we come to the details of the bill we will find grave shortcomings as result primarily of the fact that the Canada Pension Plan is not an actuarially sound funded pension plan, and that when such a plan is integrated with others that are actuarially sound on a funded basis serious inequities will be disclosed. This was predicted by many experts who gave evidence before the Canada Pension Plan committee.
The main points of my argument are these. Retired civil servants are very concerned that the proposed integration of the P.S.S.A. with the Canada Pension Plan might affect their rights. Second, they are concerned that since the Prime Minister and this present government have refused to accept any responsibility to these retired employees, that is all the more reason they should be heard. Third, I feel that because this is such a complicated matter involving the integration of complicated legislation, the integration of various civil service superannuation acts with the Canada Pension Plan it should be submitted to a special or standing committee in order that various representatives of public service organizations and public superannuation associations would be given an opportunity to present their case and hear the expert evidence.

The bill has now come back to us with clause 1, paragraph (b) which first read as follows:
The thirtieth sitting day of parliament next after the day on which any resolution of either house of parliament, based on a notice of motion in that house signed by any ten members thereof and made

in accordance with the rules of that house, that this section cease to be in force is concurred in by the other house,
The amendment from the Senate has the same effect but provides for there being a motion originated by 10 members of either house which is passed in the house and concurred in by the other house. In other words, the Senate objected to the House of Commons being solely in control of the decision and requested that it also be given the privilege of originating the motion which would bring about the end of the extension. The measure now has to be concurred in by both houses instead of only the House of Commons as originally drafted.
Motion agreed to, amendment read the second time and concurred in.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appropriate if I put on the record a few words regarding the new appointment. I will be very brief about it.
Mr. Jean-Marc Hamel of Lotbiniere, Quebec, is a graduate of Laval University. He has been in the federal public service since 1950, and I believe a great many hon. members will remember his work around the House of Commons in the staff organization work during the last two years. I am sure that those hon. members who knew him when he was director of administration on the staff of the House of Commons will be particularly well pleased with the nomination.
Since November 1965 he has been an assistant to the undersecretary of state. I for one think we are fortunate to have a man of his qualifications available to serve in this important position, because there will be much new work consequent on the redistribution of seats. I am particularly happy that Mr. Hamel is well qualified in administrative work.
I should also like to place on record a word of appreciation for the former chief electoral officer's services, and, if I may be permitted to do so, to refer to his father who preceded him in that office. For some 39 years the two Messrs. Castonguay have been the chief electoral officers of Canada. I think it would be proper for me to say we owe a word of appreciation to the father, the late Jules Castonguay, for his services from 1927 to 1949, and to Nelson Castonguay from 1949 until the present time. I always have felt that they have undertaken this work with a good understanding of the basic requirements of the job, and yet a delicacy of touch-if I may use that phrase-which is necessary in this kind of public job. I want to commend them for it.
It is interesting to note that Mr. Nelson Castonguay was responsible for the administration of the act during the last six general elections since 1949.
